31.	Major irrigation and water conservation projects in the prairie provinces, $7,500,000.

Mr. Chairman, in view of what has been said on this very important subject concerning the large project on the South Saskatchewan river, I believe I should make a few observations at this time. Irrespective of what has been said by some hon. members opposite, I am sure the Minister of Agriculture is doing all that can be done to have this great project under way as soon as possible. In saying this I know I express the feelings of the people in Rosthern constituency. During the last election campaign I told the people in that constituency about the amount of money that had been placed in the estimates for this year, and the fact they have re-elected me with an increased majority proves that they are satisfied with what is being done
This is a very important project, one that will mean much not only to Saskatchewan but to all of Canada. I am sure the minister is anxious to have this important undertaking proceeded with without delay. It surprises me to find some hon. members from my own province criticizing the minister -and I think it will be agreed that when I say "criticizing" I am putting it mildly. I believe it is the duty of each one of them to back the minister to the hilt in his efforts in connection with this project. It is such a big thing and so important that I feel it should be above party politics. I appeal to all members to support the minister in his efforts to assist Canadian farmers.

Item agreed to.
32.	Prairie Farm Assistance Act administration. $500,000.
Do the provinces make a contribution toward the payments made under this act?

The provincial governments as such contribute nothing toward the payments made under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. The taxpayers of Canada pay what is required over and above the one per cent charge on grain delivered to the elevators.

Supply-Agriculture
The levy on the farmer is the core of the fund, is it not?
No, the core of the fund is taken out of the treasury.
What are the figures on that?

About $2 is taken out of the treasury for every $1 paid in by the farmers. Those are the percentages over a period of years; but some years it is three to one and there have been years when it was four to one.
Why should not the provinces in which these payments are made contribute to this fund?
We feel that in handling it as we do the federal government is paying at least its share. If anything beyond what we are doing has to be done, then the provinces ought to pay.

Item agreed to.
33.	To provide for assistance to encourage the Improvement of cheese and cheese factories, $1,700,000.
Can the minister give us the amount of cheese now in storage and the amount that was shipped this year to Great Britain under the contract?

The amount shipped to Great Britain was 50 million pounds and the amount in store is about 17 million pounds. We do not consider that to be in the nature of a surplus, as surpluses have been discussed from time to time. It will be remembered that in 1948 it was asked whether we intended to requisition cheese, and the answer I gave was that we hoped that we would not be required to do so, that we would get the necessary deliveries of cheese without requisitioning. But we did not. There was little if any cheese delivered to us before July 21, 1948. We requisitioned cheese from that date onward, and any cheese we did obtain for the British contract was obtained through requisitions. But that did not nearly fill the British contract. I doubt very much if we would have been able to fill the British contract even though we had requisitioned right from the beginning, because at that time surplus milk was going into cans rather than into cheese.
In the spring of 1949 we were asked for permission to ship cured cheese to the United States to be sold at a higher price, but we took the position that cured cheese could be sold quite readily on this market, thus releasing more of the fresh cheese for the British market. The result was that that cured cheese was sold on this market with the result indicated. Our contract called for 50 million pounds. The British refused to take any more, and as a result there are some 17 million

pounds on our hands at present. We do not consider that a surplus, as we hope to have another contract at the beginning of the year under which we can go on delivering.
What are the production figures to date as compared with last year?
I have not the figures, but they are considerably higher.
Just how is this money used to assist cheese and cheese factories?

The assistance given to cheese producers is of two kinds. First, we pay fifty per cent of the cost of putting in storage facilities for the ageing of cheese. As most hon. members know, cheese must be kept for ninety days before being put on the market, and special storage must be provided in order to keep it properly. In an effort to encourage plants to put in the best type of storage and thus produce a better product, we have agreed to pay fifty per cent of the cost. Then we have a program of premiums of one cent on 93 score cheese and two cents on 94 score cheese.
That goes to the producer?
That goes to the producer, and also the other in an indirect way.
Did the British take all they agreed to take?
Yes.
Is the dominion government taking part in the province of Ontario scheme for the building of storage for cheese? I think $1 million is being spent this year in that way.

If it is the type of storage provided for under this item, our assistance would be given. If it is the type of storage provided for under the Cold Storage Act, organizations of a certain type would be able to get assistance. I am not so sure that we give assistance directly to the provincial governments, but we do give it to cooperatives, individuals or companies that are establishing cold storage facilities.

Item agreed to.
34.	To provide assistance for the replacement of maple production equipment, $500,000.
Where is this money being spent, and what is the explanation for the increase?

Around 1936 or 1937 the United States threatened to prevent the entry of our maple products into that country because some form of lead poisoning had been discovered. Investigations showed that

this was the result of the sap being allowed to sit in buckets which had a lead coating to prevent rust. As a result all maple products going from Canada to the United States were for some time limited in use to the manufacture of tobacco for cigarettes.
In order to overcome this difficulty, and also the possibility of lead poisoning in maple products on the Canadian market, the government agreed to a three-way plan to remove all the old equipment from the maple products industry of Quebec where most of this difficulty had been experienced. We agreed to pay one-third of the cost, the provincial government agreed to pay one-third and the producer was to accept one-third. Over the years there has been a shifting from that type of equipment to some other type, and this has not been completed.
That has been going on for how many years?

There were some expenditures in 1940-41, and these dropped in 1941-42 because of the war and our inability to obtain equipment. The expenditures were as follows:

When is this going to end? I understood a few years ago, when this item was first introduced, that over a period of years the situation would clear up. If it keeps on for many more years we shall be replacing replacements.

We do not replace replacements. One old type of equipment-perhaps I should say it was a new type-is taken out, and of course there is no further replacement of the equipment. The equipment that is being put there does not have a lead covering. Aluminum is going in in its place, and lead solder is not used. This will not be mistaken for the other. In answer to the other part of the question, it was thought when we started that we would finish this in about three years. If you will take a look at the figures I have given, you will find the amount of $300,000 for three years might have been sufficient under the circumstances. We could not get the equipment at all during the war, and therefore we could not go on with it. Now we are

taking up the slack and trying to finish it. The amount will be about the same, except that it is increased by the increase in the cost of the material.
Is production going up or down?
Production is on the increase.
What is the total amount of money that has been spent over the past number of years?
I just read the figures. The amount spent by us up to date is $964,474.64.
That means that pratically $3 million has been spent in sap buckets alone.
Not buckets alone; it is vats, boilers and everything of that kind. They had the same kind of covering.
Has any of that money been spent in eastern Ontario?
So far as I know they do not have the same problem. The difficulty was in an area of Quebec.
Surely they are not using one type of sap buckets in Quebec and another type in Ontario. Surely this situation is not going to go on and on.

There has been no application from Ontario. They are eligible if they want to apply for it. So far as I know, it is not a problem there. My memory of the sap buckets in Ontario is that they are pretty badly rusted.

Item agreed to.
35.	To provide for administrative expenses, Agricultural Prices Support Act, 1944, $60,000.

Section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act expires on March 31 of next year. Has the governor in council the power to continue the act in force without the passing of the resolution that is on the order paper?
Without the passage of the resolution on the order paper it remains as it was, which means that the government makes the decision from time to time as to what the date is.
Then all the resolution actually does is to set a cut-off date; in other words, the act expires at the end of the life of the present parliament.

The resolution does not do anything, because the minister in charge of the business of the house announced the other day that we were not putting the resolution through, so there will be no bill based upon it.

Supply-Agriculture
How much money has been spent under this act in the last year, and for what commodities?
I wonder if my friend will wait until we reach item 42, which provides the funds. This item is just administration.

Item agreed to.
36.	To reclaim and to prevent the flooding of valuable agricultural lands in the valley of the Lillooet river, near Pemberton, B.C., $312,000.
Will the minister make a brief statement about the progress of the work to date and what it is intended to do next year?
Our expectation is we will be finished with it before the end of this financial year. There is always the possibility there will be some hang-over on it, but it will not be very much.
By March 31 next?
Yes. As a matter of fact, I think it is practically completed now.
The lake has been lowered, but I understand there is still considerable ditching and diking to do in the upper areas. With winter now on, my impression is it will not be completed this year.

I understand that is in the project which is partly financed by the provinces, partly by ourselves, and partly by the individuals concerned. I am speaking from memory on that. My hon. friend probably knows the local circumstances better than I.
When we started on this project we undertook to do certain work at the expense of the federal treasury. When we had, as we thought, pretty well completed it, the province agreed to assist in the plan from there on to the extent of about one-third, generally speaking. The persons who are on the land are also bearing some of the expenditures. I believe most of that work is ditching and the other work to which reference has been made. In any case I will check it and make sure what the position is.

Item agreed to.
38. Land protection and reclamation; clearing and settlement of new lands under such terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council, $200,000.
Will the minister explain where the new lands are being brought into production?

If one reads the vote carefully, it will be seen it is not entirely confined to new lands. The first part is land protection and reclamation. Then there is a semicolon, and from there on it is another item dealing with new land. It may be used for

either purpose. It was the intention that we would be prepared to support-I think the first vote was $200,000-applications from any province where the province was prepared to pay a certain amount, and probably the individuals concerned would be charged with a certain amount. During the first two years we had no applications from anybody which conformed to the terms of the vote. This matter was discussed every year and suggestions were made that we ought to make expenditures. Last year I said if we had no applications from anyone I would not put the item in again. The result of that suggestion was that we received an application from Manitoba, and we are spending some money this year in co-operation with the government of that province. They actually take charge of the doing of the work, and we are paying dollar for dollar towards work in the Dauphin area. The Manitoba government is carrying on the operation. That is the only work that has really taken place under this provision up to the moment.

Before the item carries, I should like to ask the minister what the total expenditure has been for protection of farm lands in the Fraser valley because of damage caused by floods. From a return brought down I find that expenditures have been made by the departments of transport, public works, trade and commerce, and agriculture. The amount estimated as being required runs to more than $11 million. Will the minister make a statement as to how much money has been expended by all departments, and what further estimate is necessary to complete the work?

All I can say with regard to it is that none of the work is done under the Department of Agriculture. I presume it was done by the Department of Public Works, and some of the others. None of it was done under the Department of Agriculture, and I have no information.

Item agreed to.
40.	Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act, and necessary surveys in connection therewith, $400,000.

I should like a report from the minister as to marshland reclamation. The marsh owners are grateful to the department for what they have undertaken, but there is considerable criticism about the delay. A large amount of surveying has been done. A new superintendent, connected with prairie farm rehabilitation, has been assigned to that work. I think his name is J. S. Parker. While he was a stranger to the marshowners, and there were some misgivings as to his experience and

ability to deal with this very special work, I think he has been well received and that his plans will work out reasonably well; at least that is the hope of the marsh owners. I should like a statement from the minister as to how much money has been expended on the protection works up to the present, and I should like also a statement as to the report and representations sent in by Mr. Parker.

While the marsh-owners and general public are very appreciative of what has been done, they are somewhat critical of the delay. Some of these aboiteaux and outlets that not long ago were perhaps four feet wide and two or three feet deep in some places are now fifty feet wide and twenty-five feet deep, and the cost of repairing those breaks and protecting the land is a hundred times more than it would have been if the work could have been done when the recommendations were first made; and it is getting worse all the time. That is just in one area a few miles from the town of Amherst, where thousands of acres have been flooded.
Photographs have been forwarded to me showing storage barns with the tide about halfway up between the sills and the eaves, with the entire area flooded. That shows how urgent it is that this work be proceeded with. In that area we have the most valuable marshland in the maritime provinces, and the farmers are getting discouraged. Recently they had a meeting; they are prepared to cooperate with the department, but they want action now so that this damage will be repaired and the marshlands protected and made available to them for agricultural purposes.
IMr. Black (Cumberland).]
I would ask the minister if any decision has been arrived at with respect to the experimental station taking over certain areas of this unreclaimed land and building it up for grazing land and the production of hay. It is quite generally felt that this should be done as an example or model for the whole countryside.

As the hon. member knows, ten acres at the farm are being utilized for that purpose now. We have not contemplated taking any more land; we figured the work could be done on the ten acres, and are operating in that way.
As to the other matter, I am pleased to learn that our engineer has proved acceptable to the people and that they believe he is doing a good job. The hon. member will recall that when I was down in Nova Scotia last year there was considerable discussion as to the possibility of putting in aboiteaux as the old-timers had done perhaps a hundred years ago. They took me out to see one of these aboiteaux which I believe was put in under the direction of one of the old-timers who knew how it had been done in earlier years. He was too old himself to work on it, but he directed the operation.	They
fallowed that old method until they reached a height which they thought was above a water level that would do any damage; and when they reached that height they began to use modern equipment and methods and bulldozed the earth in.
When I was there, however, it was evident that this work was going to go out. That was an experience we had to pay for, and it was thought we should proceed more slowly until we obtained more knowledge as to how best to proceed, particularly if we are to use this modern equipment to put in these structures. In addition I understand the tide this year was the highest in the past seventy-five years, and that has been responsible for some of the damage. I quite agree, however, that if we are to avoid further damage of that kind in high tide years we must get along with the work as rapidly as possible.
As to the latter part of the question, our policy has been to take responsibility for putting in the main dike that keeps out the sea, and to that extent we have maintained certain areas as to which perhaps a definite decision has not been made with respect to how those living behind the dikes are going to handle the land, or how it will be handled by the provincial government. We figure our main job is to keep out the sea, however, and we hope to get along with that work as rapidly as possible.

If I may offer one other suggestion it would be that the department, through Mr. Parker, take steps to devise and build special machinery to excavate these small ditches the farmers used to dig by hand. It is impracticable now to get labourers to do this work; it must be done by machinery. I feel that quite large sums could be made available as an incentive to practical men, who have been accustomed to working this marshland, to devise machinery that might be useful in this work. These small ditches cannot be dug by hand at today's costs; they have to be dug by machines. So far as I know, no such equipment has been developed which is acceptable. I believe most of the owners of marshland feel that machines of this kind can be developed.

I understand that New
Brunswick has a machine which is fairly satisfactory. At the experimental farm we are working on machines which we hope will prove to be satisfactory. This development may reach a satisfactory conclusion with the support of the provincial people. I know the hon. member is acquainted with the fact that we have already purchased some machines for the larger works, such as putting in dikes. Those machines might be available.

41.	For assistance in construction of potato warehouses under regulations to be approved by the governor in council, $100,000.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister what portion of this $100,000 has been spent in the last few years on the construction of warehouses, and whether any applications for assistance have been received from the provinces.

I believe I am correct in saying that up to the moment no money has actually been spent. There was an arrangement with the province of Prince Edward Island under which we were to spend dollar for dollar with the province. The arrangement was that when that money was spent, the warehouse was to be available to the producers in the area. The province has been suggesting that its portion of the money be collected and repaid. We have not accepted that suggestion up to the moment. We have taken the position that our donation, and the provincial donation, ought to be dealt with in the same way, whichever way that is.
When the dominion put through the legislation in the first instance, there was no intention of collecting the money and returning it to the treasury. We have not asked this house for the right to collect it, and, as 45781-195
Supply-Agriculture
a result, no payments have been made in Prince Edward Island. No agreement has been reached. There are applications for assistance from New Brunswick, Ontario and Saskatchewan, in connection with the building of warehouses for the storage of potatoes. These applications are being considered.
Some warehouses have been built under the arrangement.
Some warehouses have been built, but we have not paid out any money to Prince Edward Island. We may have paid some in New Brunswick.
All the warehouses have been built in Prince Edward Island.

They have been built, but presumably they were built under directions of the provincial government. Up to the moment, we have considered that the provincial government has not carried out what we thought was the arrangement. We have not paid any money, therefore, but the warehouses are built.
From whom have the applications from New Brunswick come?
I understand the communications from New Brunswick are still in the form of requests for information about the plan. No actual application has been received as yet.

42.	Agricultural Products Act-to provide for losses incurred in respect of the purchase, sale and export of agricultural products under the Agricultural Products Act, including authority for the Minister of Finance, at the request of the Minister of Agriculture, from time to time, to pay amounts in the aggregate not exceeding $40 million out of any unappropriated money in the consolidated revenue fund as recoverable advances, $100,000.

I believe this is the appropriate item under which to ask the question I have in mind, since it deals with the export of agricultural products. It makes provision for the amount the Minister of Agriculture may call upon the Minister of Finance to supply. I believe the house should have some knowledge of the startling charge made by the Minister of Agriculture, in his reference to the export of our farm produce and other products to the United Kingdom. I have not the report from the Globe and Mail, to which the minister objected but I have the report which appeared in the Citizen and which he accepted. The headline stretched across the paper-''Startling charge by Gardiner about U.K.". It goes on to say that he addressed a board of trade dinner at Brantford, and I quote:
-he recalled that prior to the second world war, Canada was Britain's chief source of wheat and

Supply-Agriculture
apples, and also supplied considerable quantities of pork, cheese, beef and other foods. During the war Canada became Britain's chief supplier of pork, eggs and cheese, and also shipped large amounts of beef and milk.
This is the important paragraph:
"During the last two years," he said, "a very decided official effort has been made to drive every one of these products excepting wheat off the British market. And now that the four-year wheat contract is drawing to a close an effort is being made to drive off a considerable part of our wheat as well."
It seems to me that this is a serious charge. It is alleged there is an official move in Great Britain to drive Canadian products off the British market.
My understanding, from what the Prime Minister said yesterday in his discussion of the $3 million bonus for shipping losses, was that the restriction of trade between the two countries was due to the dollar shortage, and that it was our problem as much as a problem of the United Kingdom. In other words, they will have to supply us with goods in order that we may sell our farm produce overseas. I should like to remind the minister that on July 1 of this year a budgetary provision came into effect which greatly restricted the export to Canada of such things as piece goods. A few days ago I was introduced to a gentleman by one of the supporters of my hon. friend, and he told me he was the export director of a large shoe company in Great Britain. He told me that if I wanted to buy a pair of British shoes, and lived in Windsor, I could buy them cheaper in Detroit because the Canadian tariff was four times as high as the United States tariff on his product-shoes.
A short time ago I asked the minister whether the British took as much cheese as they had contracted to take, and the answer was yes. We have now lost the British market in other respects. It is true the British are looking more to the sterling areas for goods, because they have the sterling with which to buy those goods. That is not the whole story, however. Over the last two or three years I have followed this trade matter rather carefully.
Take, for example, the position as to bacon. The minister has often said that we supplied Britain with vast quantities of bacon during and since the war. In 1948 the British expected 195

million pounds, but we failed to deliver anything like that amount. I believe the contract this year is for 160 million pounds, and according to a return that was tabled in the house, we sent only 14 million pounds in the first three months of the year.

On page 3 of their report, dealing with trade up to the end of September, I found that we had exported to Great Britain about 28 million pounds of bacon. It seems to me that unless the minister can tell the house what the official action of which he complains is, a statement of this kind is something to which objection should be taken by all members of this House of Commons. It certainly does not make for good relationships. The minister will recollect that in 1948 we agreed to send 195 million pounds of bacon. We also agreed to send a quantity of beef. We are losing the United Kingdom market, and we are losing it for two reasons.
We have lost it.

All right; that is the hon. member's opinion. I will not go that far. I think we are losing it for two reasons. One is our failure to fulfil understandings of such importance to the British people. The second, of course, is the maintenance of a relatively high tariff. When the Geneva agreements were made two years ago some of us in the house urged the government to use one of the escape clauses in the agreement so that we would not have to put into effect immediately the non-discrimination clauses in the treaty. As hon. members will recall, we had a year's grace; and if the exchange situation was bad, we could ask for a further

extension of time. But the government put the whole treaty or agreement into effect immediately; and may I say that while that agreement has been on the order paper it has never been ratified by the House of Commons.
The committee should have a knowledge of the facts on which the minister based this statement. If there is an official attitude to drive Canadian products off the British market, he should take the committee into his confidence. This is a serious matter. It is particularly serious because of the manner in which Canada went to the assistance of the overseas countries during the war, and because of the manner in which we changed our economy in many respects during the war to meet the overseas needs. I think the people of Canada should know on what the minister's statement is based.
If, on the other hand-and this appears to me to be so from all that I can read- this stems purely, or mainly, from a dollar shortage, then I think that Canada should endeavour to co-operate with the sterling and other areas and should endeavour, through international organization, to set up a plan whereby we might bring about the convertibility of our various currencies, or even go to the extent of finding an international currency that would enable us to trade with one another. After all, the world is short of food-it is always short of food- and Canada is a great potential provider of food. If we lose the only markets we have, and there is no possibility of finding sufficient new markets, what will be the condition in this country within a few years?
I greatly regretted that Canada did not support the proposal made recently at the United Nations for dealing with surplus foods. I notice that the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Mr. H. Hannam, was of much the same opinion. He said recently:
Farmers want some assurance of stability in markets projected ahead a few years to enable them to plan their production with confidence. With this view, we found the farmers of all countries in complete agreement.
He went on further to say:
Our Canadian federation put a proposal for moving embarrassing surpluses into consumption before the international federation of agricultural producers at Guelph and it was unanimously endorsed. It proposed the setting up of an international agency and fund to take surpluses, arrange for their sale to needy people at special prices, and have the loss shared between the fund and the supplying country.
That may not apply to our trade relationships with Great Britain, but it does apply to dealing with potential surpluses of foodstuffs in this country in the next two years.

I have here a statement which appeared in the press of December 7, under the heading, "Coldwell claims session proving promises false". It says:
"There are others," he added. "For instance, a couple of weeks ago our Minister of Agriculture, Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, opposed the United Nations proposal for feeding the world's hungry with food surpluses . . ."
That is the kind of statement, of course, which one might expect politically, but it ought to be based upon the facts. The facts as they have been given to this house over and over again, and over and over again to the country, and as every paper in Canada that I have been reading has published them, are that up until 1947 every representative of the British government who came here was bent upon securing all the food they could from Canada, and entered into contracts with us, which were fully understood by them, and fully understood by us, and fully reported to the house on every occasion.
I stated as early as 1939, and every session after that, that until the time the war started, the British did not believe we could produce in Canada enough foods of the types they required. Certainly they did not believe that we could produce bacon for the British people in any greater quantity than about 160 million pounds. We maintained that we could produce more than that, as the Conservatives before us had maintained that we could.

Mr. Bennett secured under the Ottawa agreements of 1932-written into those agreements -a figure of 280 million pounds of bacon. There was no way in which Canada could contract to deliver it, because under our federal system of government we have no authority to compel delivery to us.
So there was no opportunity for the government to make use of what other countries are able to make use of, namely, making a direct contract with the British government, and then compelling delivery to carry it out. We were not able to do that. But when the war came along we were able to do it. We compelled delivery under the War Measures Act.
Before the Canadian government entered into contract with the British government we stated over and over again at food conferences that we were going to prove conclusively to the British people that we could produce any possible amount they could take from us. I recall we produced over 700 million pounds in one year, when we had been told before that they were not going to expect more than 160 million, the quota insisted upon in 1936 under the Ottawa agreement. But when we battled under the preceding government and battled under this government we induced them to put the figure up to 280 million. By the time the war started we had almost reached 280 million pounds. After the war did start, by signing contracts with the British for 50 million pounds a year more than our officials estimated the farmers could produce, and more than the British expected to get from us, in every year we exceeded the contract. We exceeded it by more than 50 million pounds, until we got up to over 700 million pounds shipped over there within one twelve-months period.
When we got to that point the British government sent a man to this country, Mr. Scott Watson. He appeared before the farm associations, sometimes behind closed doors. I was present at the first meeting in Regina, when he made a speech behind closed doors. I think the words he used were, in effect, that when the war was over it would be necessary to trade bicycles for bacon in Denmark.

Representative of the ministry of agriculture in the government of Great Britain, and he still is an important official in connection with that same department.

I think most of them thought that they could find a way of financing these purchases. However, in the fall of 1947 that policy was changed. I am not going to attempt to say who changed it; hon. members can come to just as reliable a conclusion on that as I can, because they know what changes were made at that time. One of the outstanding changes was that we were told that there was great difficulty in finding dollars with which to pay for our food.
Was not that true?

It may have been true, but it did not give a basis for the statement that has been made that we have not been squeezed out of the British market. The delegation that came here in the fall of 1947 stated, in so many words, that they did not want any food products except wheat at any price, and that they wanted wheat at the price they were paying under the contract. We naturally said, and it has been reported to this house although not in as definite terms as I am stating it now-I think it is time it should be stated definitely-that if there was going to be no contract, there was going to be none. That meant that all our foods would have to be sold at the world market price. From that time on an effort was made to take more of our foods; but no matter how much discussion we had about it, it finally came down to the fact that they were prepared to take only cheese, bacon and eggs and in the quantities which we were certain we could send forward in spite of anything that might happen elsewhere.
We sat down as a result of that understanding and tried to figure the quantities but not as we had done earlier in the war. We could not go out to the farmers, as we had gone then, and tell them how much to produce to the limit for a market which existed. We figured it down to the last pound which we thought we had to get rid of in order to make it possible for our farmers to go on marketing at all in this

country, even at reasonable price levels. I think everyone will realize that if you put back on this market 86 million dozen eggs; if you threw back on this market even the quantity of bacon we did send to Great Britain, or if you threw back on this market any of those other farm products, you would have lower prices, which might be beneficial to some people but would not be beneficial to the farming population.
We decided that the furthest we could go was to get rid of what we might feel was going to be a surplus. We agreed with the British-it was not put into writing-that we would cut that down as low as we could throughout the whole twelve months. In other words, we would sell all the products we could somewhere else, on the Canadian market or the United States market or somewhere else, provided that we could get at least as good a price for them as we had written into the contracts. We would go ahead and sell them, and if we sold them all we would not deliver anything to Great Britain. That is as they wanted it. I have no hesitation in saying that, no matter what anyone anywhere else may say. That is as they wanted it. They wanted those quantities reduced in the year 1948 down to nothing at all. There was no way of going out to the farmers of this country and telling them to produce more for the British market or more for the United States market; we had to be careful about what we said.
When we got along to the next year the British came and said: "We will take wheat and cheese, but we do not want anything else." There is no doubt about what they said. This matter has been reported both overseas and here and discussed quite fully. They said that they could not finance these purchases. Probably I am going a little too far in saying that they said they did not want them. Of course the British would like to have more food of certain types. They said they could not finance it, and for economic reasons they did not want it. They said that they did not want any. There is no doubt about how much it was; it was none at all.
We then said to them: "We can sell our cheese in the United States for more than what is proposed; why should you want to take only cheese." I am not going to suggest that that was the reason; nevertheless we were told that they could find dollars with which to buy cheese without depending upon ECA, but they could not find dollars with which to buy anything else without depending upon ECA. Under great pressure they finally agreed to make a contract for some 46 million dozen eggs, none of it in fresh shelled egg form. The price of shelled eggs in Poland, Denmark or any other country compared with ours does not mean anything. They did not agree to take any of our fresh shelled eggs at any price, and we have had to market them as best we could in the United States and Canada. I might say that up to now we have done a fairly good job of getting them marketed.

You can put it whichever way you like. They have much more to do with settling that question than we have.

They said that under the multilateral contract which was being discussed then they considered that a reasonable acreage for their farmers to have in wheat; and they went on to say that they considered the acreage to which we had reduced ourselves during the war to be a reasonable acreage for our farmers to have. At the time that was said I believe we had something like 22 million acres of land in wheat. In our contracts of that time we went on to provide that other nations, in order to avoid these surpluses, had to reduce their acreage if they were to come in under those contracts.
At the end of the war all agreements of that kind were taken out of the contracts, and they are not now in the contracts at all. There is no acreage control in the contracts.
When I went down to the United States I was of the opinion that probably the Americans still wanted to go on producing that great acreage of wheat. If they did, it was going to cause us trouble. Some representatives of the other nations proposed that the Americans should continue producing that extra quantity of wheat, but the United States representative disagreed with them. He said the United States did not think it should continue to do so, not only in the interests of their present agricultural position, but in the interests of the long-term food position in the world. In other words it was said by the United States: If we keep several million acres in grain, eventually the soil will be blowing around and will not be producing anything. The United States representatives were of the opinion the soil should be turned back into grass and the production of livestock and other products.
Immediately I rose and agreed with them. That is what I was doing when I got the report which indicated that I might have been doing something else. I agreed with the United States people, and pointed out the reason for doing so, namely, that Canada has practically no surplus of wheat at the moment. I said that as a matter of fact we had not surpluses, to the extent we had before the war, in any agricultural products. The

Supply-Agriculture
reporter called them "top-heavy surpluses"; he said that I said we did not have any top-heavy surpluses. This was a fair interpretation of what I had been saying.
As a result of this discussion-at least I presume partly as a result of it, and partly as a result of their own judgment-when the United States representatives made their proposal to the conference it included a reduction in the acreage that was to be put into grain. I had a discussion with some of our press representatives at Washington as to whether "grain" meant wheat. One of them went to interview the leader of the United States delegation, Mr. Andrews. A report of that interview appears in the Regina Leader-Post, and I am going to read a paragraph or two of it, just to indicate why we think that we were on the right line:
Mr. Andrews said that the acreage devoted to wheat in the United States had risen by approximately 26 million from the low point of 55 million before the war. This increase was roughly equal to the acreage sown by Canada on its entire wheat crop. Mr. Andrews was fully aware of the anxiety this enlarged United States crop must cause to Canadian farmers seeking an outlet for their own produce.
Strictly on U.S. grounds of policy, however. Mr. Andrews was convinced that a new policy had to be applied. Much of this wheat was being grown on land never intended for this purpose. It had been brought into cultivation under the stress of the war and post-war needs. If it were not returned to grass, then "the land would blow away."
Already the U.S. government had made a start on this program by ordering a reduction of fourteen per cent in last year's wheat acreage of 81 million. Mr. Andrews expressed the private opinion that total reductions in the next three years might amount to something like 25 million acres.
That is exactly what we had in mind when we went there. We wanted to bring that situation about, and the Americans are stating that it is their intention anyway, no matter what we think about it. To continue:
Mr. Andrews said the government had two great sanctions in existing legislation to enforce this policy. These were acreage allotments and market quotas for individual farmers. Any farmer could store wheat on his farm, but if he tried to market wheat above his quota he might be fined very severely, in some cases up to fifty per cent of the value of his wheat. Restricting these allotments and quotas was one way to cut down on wheat acreage.
Then this reporter goes on to say that, so far as the farmers of western Canada are concerned, that was the most important accomplishment of the FAO conference. I believe it was more important to have that wheat acreage reduction, and the land used for other purposes, than that our farmers should be forced out of wheat in order to maintain a surplus which might be of assistance to people somewhere else, but would

put our farmers in a worse condition economically than the people we are trying to help.
That is the only report that I care to make at the moment in connection with the matter, in view of the fact the official report of the position taken by the Canadian government is not yet in my hands.

I have heard a long list of editorials that have appeared in different papers, but I am asking about memoranda or correspondence. Editorial opinion is the opinion of one man who is writing for a newspaper. We know what editorial opinion is.

If you are not interested in editorial opinion, all I can say is that every official from the city of Ottawa, and every official who came from Britain, knows that every word I have uttered is correct, and that includes every member of the government who is sitting in this house. That is a correct statement of what took place. I do not believe it needs any backing from anyone else, except those who were present, and they were the only people who heard it.

The minister's statement is all the greater indication as to why the Minister of Trade and Commerce should make a long-term agreement with the United States. We might as well forget about the United Kingdom. I am surprised that the Minister of Trade and Commerce went down to New York and told the people they should buy from Europe. He should have been telling the people of the United States that they should buy from Canada. He should have been making a long-term agreement with the United States. We might as well make up our minds that the 175 million people on the North American continent will have to live within themselves.
Just to set the record straight, I may say that I was in the United States to tell them that if they did not buy more from Canada, then Canada would not be able to buy as much from them.

The minister told them
they should buy from Europe, and Donald Gordon, an employee of this government, told them they should buy from Europe.

Mr. Chairman, the speech that has just been made by the Minister of Agriculture is one of the most significant utterances that has been made in this house for many years. He has used phrases that are bound to have an important effect on the relationship between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom. As members of this house we must

assume that this speech is a carefully prt pared statement of the position of this government and its attitude towards the dealings they have had, and expect' to have, with the government of the United Kingdom in regard to agricultural products.
So far as we are concerned, the export of agricultural products to the United Kingdom is by far our most important export. The statement the minister has just made, therefore, is one that may have a far-reaching effect in considering the future of that export market. This market was described by the members and by the Minister of Trade and Commerce just a few days ago as being vital to the future of this country. On December 1 the Minister of Trade and Commerce used these words at page 2551 of Hansard:
Canada's prosperity is dependent to a large extent on the state of world trade and more particularly on our trade with the United Kingdom and the United States, our two largest suppliers as well as our two largest customers.
What we have just heard is a statement that there is a deliberate onslaught by the government of the United Kingdom on our trade in farm product's with that country. Surely it is not possible to imagine a statement of more significance, a more serious statement, if that does interpret the situation correctly.
One of the reasons why this statement must be of great concern to every hon. member is the impression that is left by what we have now heard as compared with the impression that was left on the minds of the members of the house and other Canadians who read the reports of the statements made here, right up to December 1. Hon. members who were in the house on that day will recall that when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was being asked certain questions in regard to the sale of food products in Britain, and particularly in regard to some of the very food products that the Minister of Agriculture has now mentioned, he left the impression that there was no reason for concern about the future sales of those products. In his speech on December 1, 1949, as reported at page 2571 of Hansard, after giving a number of figures which showed our large export of food products to the United Kingdom in the present year and in recent years, he used these words:
Judging from these figures I have quoted one would hardly reason that we are losing our trade with Britain. Let us take the individual commodities. What about wheat? I think we are in grave danger of being oversold on wheat from this crop.
Those words, Mr. Chairman, do not give anything like the same impression as the words that we have just heard from the Minister of Agriculture, who is primarily 45781-196J
Supply-Agriculture
charged with the responsibility for supervising production of these particular commodities. The Minister of Trade and Commerce did not confine his optimistic remarks to wheat. He spoke of oats, barley, flax, bacon and other food products. Nor should I limit my reference to the recent statement on December 1 of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. On May 12 of this year I find that the Regina Leader-Post carried an extended report of a speech of the Minister of Agriculture in Simpson, Saskatchewan, under the heading: "Market is safe, Gardiner says". Then, criticizing those who had suggested that there was reason for concern about our markets in the United Kingdom, he used these words, according to the Regina Leader-Post:
We could sell much more of most farm products if we had them in surplus supply.
I could give numerous quotations which show that right up to December 1, both outside and inside the house, ministers of the crown have sought to create the impression that, in spite of disturbing incidents and difficulties that were being encountered, our market in the United Kingdom is safe, to use the words that were attributed to the Minister of Agriculture last May. If in this important speech of his this morning the Minister of Agriculture had told the members of this committee that, to his great surprise, he had just learned that there was a resistance to the purchase of Canadian commodities in the United Kingdom, and that, to his amazement, the government of the United Kingdom is conducting a deliberate onslaught on the sale of these Canadian commodities in the United Kingdom, then certainly we would have reason to be astonished and alarmed by such a statement; but at least it would be an explanation of the difference between the statement we have just heard and the statements that have been made outside and inside this chamber until recent days.
To me one of the most revealing features of the speech of the Minister of Agriculture is the fact that he tells us of a meeting behind closed doors in Regina in 1947, and he tells us that in 1947-
May I just say that the meeting was reported in the press; what I said was reported in the press the next day.
Nevertheless it was reported in the press at that time without such an interpretation as is now put upon it by the Minister of Agriculture.
No. I put the same interpretation on it then myself.

Oh, no. If the Minister of Agriculture put such an interpretation on it at that time, it is extremely difficult to

Supply-Agriculture
understand why he was saying last May that our markets in the United Kingdom were safe, or why the Minister of Trade and Commerce was saying in this chamber on December 1 that we had every reason for confidence in the United Kingdom market.
That was before the election.

The statement in May of course was before the election. But what the Minister of Agriculture now says-and he cannot be critical of the reference to what he himself has told us this morning-is that in Regina in 1947 an official of the British government informed this meeting that in his opinion the United Kingdom would not be buying our foodstuffs in any event, and that, to repeat the illustration which he used, the United Kingdom would be trading bicycles for Danish bacon. If that is so, and if the minister has been aware that there was a deliberate onslaught on our sale of food products to the United Kingdom, then what I find extremely difficult to understand is how it was possible for him to continue to assure the Canadian farmers of the advantages they were gaining by contracts under which they were receiving less than the world price because of the assured long-term markets at those prices at a time when, he suggested, world prices might be less than they then were. The key to the alleged value of those agreements was the assurance that the contracts would be the basis of continued prices at that level, and that, while Canadian farmers might not at that time be receiving the world prices, they would later receive more than the world prices.
Nor was it possible to listen to the remarks made by the Minister of Agriculture this morning without remembering where he made the speech that he made a few days ago. It was not made to an agricultural group.
Fifty-fifty.
It was made in the city of Brantford, which is a very important industrial city.
At a board of trade meeting.
I am aware there would doubtless be many farmers there. I am not suggesting for one moment that this speech was not fully reported both in the press of Canada and in the press of the United Kingdom.
Just to keep the record straight, may I say it was rural night for the board of trade. They had invited the farmers to come in and listen to the speaker, and I had been invited to speak.

It was in Brantford, an important industrial centre, from which there comes

a great deal of agricultural equipment. The farmers in the Brantford area are responsive to the concern that might be felt by their immediate local market about the future of industrial production in that area.
The minister has said that his speech was given a fairly good reception in Brantford, and that it has received favourable comment from elsewhere since then. Certainly it would receive a favourable response from one point of view, and a perfectly natural point of view. He was asserting the proposition that, as Canadians, our first concern must be for Canada, and, quite properly, that our trade relationships with the United Kingdom or with any other country must be based upon our own legitimate self-interest.
The suggestion that Canadian purchases of industrial products from Britain should be related to Britain's willingness to buy agricultural products from us would undoubtedly receive support. I am not questioning the fact that it should receive support. But what we have been told today is that the reason for concern about the United Kingdom market is not something that arises now, but something that has been present since 1947 at least. That, to me, is one of the very real reasons for concern in connection with what we have heard here this morning.
It is difficult, if not impossible, to escape the impression that the Minister of Agriculture is now seeking to hide behind the government of the United Kingdom for the purpose of explaining the optimistic statements which have been made for the last two years, and which do not gibe with what he has told us now about the attitude of the government of the United Kingdom as disclosed at Regina, and as disclosed, according to his statement, at every subsequent meeting they have had.
The minister now tells us that our difficulties are not so much related to the dollar problem as they are to this deliberate onslaught upon our sale of products in the United Kingdom. I would remind hon. members that when I use the expression "deliberate onslaught" I am using the words employed here today by the Minister of Agriculture. He left no doubt that in his mind this is not so much a problem of dollars as it is a question of deliberate policy on the part of the government of the United Kingdom. He has emphasized that belief by saying that, after all, the solution of the dollar problem is much more the problem of the United Kingdom than it is for us.
By those very words the minister supported the clear statement he had made that this is a question of government policy. No matter what any one of us here may think of the

political point of view of the present government in the United Kingdom, it is the present government of the United Kingdom; it is the government of that country chosen by the people of that country. Therefore we must regard a statement of this kind as having the utmost importance. Because the Minister of Agriculture did explain why he made that statement in Brantford-and in this I am referring to a report contained in the Ottawa Journal of December 6, which states:
He was talking about it just now because negotiations for new food contracts with the United Kingdom are approaching conclusion. All existing food contracts, except that for cheese, expire the end of this month.
If that press report is a correct interpretation of what he said, either in his formal remarks or otherwise, then the Minister of Agriculture explained that he was making a speech at that time in which he was sharply critical of the government of the United Kingdom because negotiations for new food contracts with the United Kingdom were approaching a conclusion.
I can only interpret those words as meaning that the Minister of Agriculture was making this speech as part of the broad negotiations that were taking place, and that the purpose of the speech was to have its influence upon those negotiations. If that is so, and if his speech here this morning is for the same purpose, then it does unquestionably place before the government and people of the United Kingdom the proposition that, in the opinion of the government of Canada, the government of the United Kingdom has decided not to buy, no matter how much the people of that country like or approve the taste, standards or general quality of the food products they get from Canada.
This is something they should know. I agree with that proposition. By all means let us discuss these matters out in the open. By all means let us have all the essential facts before it is too late. If the situation is the one placed before us this morning, then it will be a good thing if, before the conclusion of these present contracts, the people of the United Kingdom have an opportunity to express their opinion as to what they think the government of that country should do.
I would also hope that in the interests of having a full knowledge of the facts, the appropriate official or officials of the government of the United Kingdom will say whether or not in their opinion the statement given to us this morning does correctly represent the situation. Unless we have that statement of course we cannot know what hope there may be of working out arrangements for the future.	[DOT]

I am not going to go into the details of the many figures that were presented to us this morning by the Minister of Agriculture in his long speech. I say long speech, but I admit that this important statement by the minister certainly required to be made, and adequate time had to be taken to give the essential details. In that speech the minister has left the responsibility for the present situation on the doorstep of the government of the United Kingdom. He has. left the impression that the dollar problem is not the crux of the problem that we have to solve; that the government of the United Kingdom, as a matter of continuing policy, is making an onslaught on our sales of food products in that country.
This being so, I suggest that, apart from the other considerations that have been put forward, there should be in the mind of every one of us the realization that this is either a problem attached to currency difficulties or it is not. I would remind hon. members of the fact that on several occasions recently it has been pointed out that currency problems are at the root of some of our difficulties. One recalls that in the excellent report of the maritime commission tabled in the house not long ago, it was stated that the recommendations they made would not help to solve the problems connected with shipping or the shipping industry unless there was a solution of the currency problem. We have heard that said inside and outside of this house in relation to other questions of trade.
The word "convertibility" has been used in this discussion. I suggest that the real crux of this problem is convertibility, and this is a problem that can be tackled by the Canadian government, because it is not exclusively a problem of the government of the* United Kingdom. Unless our trade in foodstuffs and other products is to be seriously threatened, one of the things most urgently required is that the government of the United Kingdom and the government of Canada get together to see if it is not possible to find some basis of actual convertibility which will loosen this log-jam and avoid the possibility of an extremely serious trade situation in the not distant future.
I suggest that everything that has been said here this morning emphasizes the need of tackling that problem. I suggest that everything that has been said here this morning emphasizes the importance of checking carefully what has been said in the past, and insisting upon the most complete and accurate information as to what is the present situation.
I can only repeat that what we have been told this morning is inconsistent with the

statement made to this house in regard to these very products as recently as December 1. In the discussion that may take place now, between now and the next session and again at that time, we will insist upon full information. I would hope that the other party to the contracts, the government of the United Kingdom, will assist us in placing fully before the public, and in that way before us, their explanation of the present problem. Only in this way can a solution be found.
What has been said here this morning is significant and most serious. I feel sure that all hon. members want to retain these markets, and it is to be hoped that in seeking a favourable outcome of the negotiations which are taking place in regard to the renewal of these contracts a barrier of misunderstanding will not be created between the government of Canada and the government of the United Kingdom.
One o'clock.
I understood that we were to go right along.

I was not aware that we were -going to go right through. I would point out that we still have to consider the estimates of trade and commerce, public works, finance, justice, the Prime Minister's office and legislation, all in full. We have still some items in agriculture, veterans affairs, and mines and resources. I take it it is up to the committee to consider whether it is possible to do that amount of work properly between now and midnight tonight. If it is, then I have no objection to sitting right through, but if it is not, I think we should adjourn for lunch. I am doubtful myself as to the possibility of completing all those departments before midnight.	[DOT]

So that our position may be known to the committee I want to make it quite clear that we did agree to sitting through until six o'clock tonight. I certainly will not withdraw in any way from that agreement. I think it was hoped by all members that it would be possible to complete business by this afternoon, but I must say that at the present time there does not seem to be the slightest possibility of that being done. I do not think there is the slightest possibility of the business now before us being completed today, even though we sit through until midnight without interruption.
The opposition can assume no responsibility for the amount of time that is involved. There are still three important departments to be dealt with. The Minister of Agriculture spoke for an hour and ten minutes this

morning, and needed that time for the important statement he made. However, it is perfectly obvious, in view of the importance of the statement whi'ch was made here for the first time this morning, the significance of which hon. members cannot be expected to disregard, they should not be limited in any way in their discussion of it.
I have mentioned this in order to point out that I do not suggest that any undertaking be withdrawn, but the undertaking was on the premise that we would complete the business. If there is general agreement that that cannot be done by six o'clock, it would seem the most sensible procedure to recognize that fact and adjourn. Then we would be able to resume on Monday without being unduly exhausted by the effort made today to accomplish the impossible.
I have no objection to sitting right through if it is believed that we can finish the business.
