I want to reply to part of what was said by the leader of the opposition. Whether my statement was long or short, it was not a statement in which I was attempting to say what the reasons were for the position that was taken by the British. I was asked a definite question. I was asked to prove to the satisfaction of the leader of the C.C.F. group, and I presume others who think likewise, that there had been some official opposition to the marketing of these products in Great Britain. When he asked me if that was not owing to the dollar question, I said probably in part, but that after all that' was a British responsibility as much as, or more than, it was ours. I was not discussing that question at the time.
As to the remarks that were made by the leader of the official opposition, I only wish
Supply-Agriculture
to say that I take nothing back concerning that question from what I said a year ago. All that is on record, and I do not think it is necessary to repeat it.
On the other question of what was said before and after the election, my remarks both before and since the election were exactly the same as they were when I was in London a year ago. The newspaper reports naturally did not repeat everything I said, and every speech I delivered, over and over again. They took certain parts out of them and printed them.
So far as the speech at Simpson and speeches anywhere else are concerned, I stated that at the end of this season there would not be any of the surpluses of farm products which our opponents were prophesying we would have. I said our wheat would be all gone. I said we would not be able to fill our bacon contract, we would not be able to fill our egg contract, and all our food would have disappeared, with the possible exception of cheese, as to which we had already realized that the British would not take any further quantities. We have never expected any difficulty in connection with cheese. Therefore there is no difference between what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been saying and what I have been saying.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said about the beginning of the year that we had no troublesome surpluses. I said in Washington that we have no top-heavy surpluses. There is no difference between those statements; they mean exactly the same thing. I was reported to have said in Washington that there are no top-heavy surpluses. I did not use the word "top-heavy", but it states, as well as any one word could, what I did say.

In view of what the minister has just said, why did he find it necessary to refer to the British as making an onslaught? If someone has made an onslaught on our trade, it suggests that everything in the garden is not so lovely.

I do not know of any other word to describe it, and I am not withdrawing it. When we met with them in the fall of 1947 they said they did not want our food products except wheat. The second time they visited us, in 1948, they included cheese, but they did not include cheese in 1947. They said: We prefer not to have these products. As a matter of fact, at certain stages they said they would not take these products, and at certain stages we said other things which induced them to take the products. I do not think it is necessary to repeat all that here

Supply-Agriculture
Then why were understandings reached in a given year? We will take 1947. There were 195 million pounds of bacon-
That was before.

-plus 29 million pounds of bacon later on, making 224 million pounds which they agreed to take, but we delivered only 176 million. Going back to 1946, the contract was for 450 million pounds, and we delivered far short of that amount. Coming to the present year, they said they would take 160 million pounds of bacon, and up to the end of September we have delivered approximately 58 million pounds. It simply does not make sense.
I have not applied anything I said to any time prior to the fall of 1947. I made that very clear. I indicated that under all members of the British government-
What about this year?

Let me answer what the hon. member has already asked. Until the fall of 1947 we had complete understanding with the members of the government in Great Britain. It does not matter whether it was the Churchill government or the present government. We have always made it clear that this is not a matter of party differences, either in Britain or here or anywhere else. So far as I am concerned it is simply a matter of fact.
Until we got to the fall of 1947 we had complete understandings to the effect that we would market our surpluses of bacon, cheese, eggs and other products in Great Britain. I am dealing only at the moment, however, with bacon, cheese and eggs; those other products were included prior to that time. Well, we set out to do that. At the same time we were increasing the purchasing power of our own people, and I have said over and over again that our people now are buying as much as fifty per cent more meat for their own consumption than they bought before the war. I have taken credit to the government, as has been stated, for evolving policies which brought about that result. Whether we are entitled to all the credit I have taken may be a question; nevertheless I say we have assisted in creating conditions which have resulted in Canadians consuming more and more of those products. That was what I was emphasizing at Simpson and at every other meeting I attended, namely, that we have created better conditions by family allowances, old age pensions and all the other social services, and by other methods which I went into at the time.
Having done that; with Canadians themselves-including the farmers-buying so much more food in Canada, the amounts we sent to Britain under the contracts were reduced from year to year up to 1947. Until that time we could go to the farmers and tell them to produce more and more; but since that time, as I said, we have not been telling the farmers to produce more and more. The reasons I gave were the very reasons I have given this house today, namely, that we had already been told by the British that they did not want these products. I have always said on those occasions that their reason for not wanting them was a dollar reason. It was not because they did not want our food; it was because they were not able to finance the payment for it.
That can hardly be described as a deliberate onslaught.

I think it is a deliberate onslaught when officials come to you year after year, as they did in 1947 and again in 1948, and as they are doing now, and say: "We do not want your food at all." What are you going to call it, if it is not a deliberate onslaught? At the same time they say: "We are still going to buy that food, but in some other area." Sometimes they even come to this continent and buy the food in another area, paying for it in dollars. I do not know of any other term to describe it than a deliberate attempt to stop buying in this area. I presume it is because they cannot find the dollars with which to pay for it; but the attempt is deliberate.
That is different language.

I do not know any other word for it. The fact is that our farmers must realize, as we are going into another crop year, that this is the attitude with regard to the shipment of food to Great Britain at the present time.
On the other question, whether or not we have surpluses, I have been saying that we have none, and I am prepared to say now that we have none. The only commodity in which there appears to be a surplus is cheese, and I have explained that, so I need not go into it further. So far as the Minister of Trade and Commerce and myself are concerned, we are in entire agreement that we have not surpluses. On the other hand we have not been selling our products to Britain even in the quantities in which we sold them before the war; and they would prefer that we did not sell them any.

I regret very much that there seems to be danger of friction developing between this country and Great Britain in connection with our trade. I must say there

has been a real change in attitude on the part of the Minister of Agriculture as between today and a year ago. I believe he outlined the situation clearly in a speech he made before the Canadian chamber of commerce in London in December, 1948. His attitude was very different, of course, during the election campaign. X will agree that the stand he has taken today is the same as the one he took before the Canadian chamber of commerce, but it is not the same as the one he took while the election campaign was on.
You did not hear any of my speeches. My position was just the same.

I read a number of them, and I heard a great deal about them. When X would discuss government policy at meetings, people would get up and quote statements by the minister on the trade position, in which he said there was no danger of the food contracts with Britain falling off. These statements were thrown at me time and again during the campaign, and my only reply was to quote what the minister had said in addressing the Canadian chamber of commerce in London.
Both the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce have pointed out time and again that the situation that is developing is largely due to the fact that the United Kingdom lacks dollars with which to buy our produce. It is not a question, of course, of Britain not wanting to buy our goods. The people there want our goods, but they have not the dollars. They have to buy their goods now where they can get them without spending dollars; so that the word "want" is ambiguous in that sense.
I agree with the minister that the official attitude of the British government today is that they must cut down their imports from Canada in order to conserve dollars. On the other hand I am satisfied that if they had the dollars they would be anxious to buy goods from us.
Another point is that the action the British government is taking today has been recommended by the international monetary fund and the administration of Marshall aid. They have been told time and again they must do everything in their power to cut down imports from the dollar area. You may find that in the annual report of the international monetary fund for 1948. So they are only doing what they have been advised to do by the body we helped set up, in an attempt to bring about a closer balance of trade. I think it only natural that they should take that action, because Marshall aid ends in 1952. The only reason why various nations
Supply-Agriculture
have been able to buy the quantity of goods they have taken from us is that they have been given dollars with which to buy them.

May I say to my hon. friend at this point, if he does not mind, that I think he will agree, as I believe most hon. members will agree, that no one has backed the British since 1939 more than I have as Minister of Agriculture in this country. No one has said more kind things about them or has more fully appreciated the British position than I have. But when it comes to the facts as they are related to our own farmers, then I think those facts have to be stated. My kindly feelings towards the British cannot be allowed to run so far that the farmer does not know his position. I think he must know that.
I think it will be generally agreed that all through the period under discussion, from 1947 to the present time, the people of Canada have pretty well known the British position. At no time during the election campaign did I say we were sure of being able to get contracts with Britain. I did indicate what had happened in the past. I said the British had come to every meeting and said they did not want our food, but that in spite of the fact that they said they did not want it we were able to get contracts for quantities which have worked out to our satisfaction, and I was hopeful that in future we would be able to do the same thing. We are now in the midst of making contracts for the third time under those conditions, and we are still hopeful that we shall be able to obtain contracts covering some of the foods, though not all of them, or even all for which we had contracts last year. We hope to get those contracts for next year; and my hope, which X presume is the hope of the hon. member who was speaking a moment ago, is that by that time Britain may have the dollars with which to buy more of our products. I do not know how they are going to get there, but I do think the British want our food, in the sense the term has been used by the hon. member. They are going to insist on having it, no matter what government they have, as soon as they have the means to pay for our food. Xt is mainly for that reason that I want to keep the products in the British market under these agreements, until the British can get back into that position.

I do not take any exception to the speeches the minister has been making. I believe he has been quite clear, although some people have the impression from his speeches that he is hostile to the British over this market situation. If one takes all the minister's speeches, both the ones delivered

Supply-Agriculture
in Great Britain and in this country, I think one gets the correct impression. I have always felt that the Minister of Agriculture felt rather kindly towards Britain, and would do anything he could to extend our trade with that country.
The minister has pointed out that the situation that has developed is due to a lack of dollars. I take direct issue with the minister when he tries to put the blame for that situation on Britain. Just a few moments ago the minister said that the shortage of dollars was Britain's responsibility. I should like him to show me any way in which the shortage of dollars is Britain's responsibility.
That is hardly correct. What I said meant the possibility of its being corrected is more likely to be through Britain's efforts than through anything we can do.

Right after the war, in order to get aid from the United States, Britain signed the Bretton Woods agreement, and also agreed to make sterling convertible, knowing full well she could not carry out that agreement. After a few weeks of attempting to do it, Britain was forced off convertibility. We now have the unpleasant situation under which she cannot get the dollars she needs for her business.
When members suggest that a possible solution to this difficulty would be the establishment of convertible currency, or the establishment of an international currency, it seems to me they are putting the cart before the horse. You might have convertibility of currencies, but until you establish a balance of trade you will not get very far. The establishment of an international currency would not mean that all nations would be able to buy. The only way a nation could get that currency would be by selling its goods to another nation, and taking payment in international currency. So long as you have the unfavourable balance of trade in the sterling area which you have today, there will be a shortage of dollars with which to buy goods. An international currency would not be any solution to the difficulty, because you would still have an unbalance of trade between the sterling area and the dollar area.
The only solution for the problem is for the sterling area to adopt the attitude that the Minister of Trade and Commerce seems to have adopted towards the United States. He has said that, so far as Canada and the United States are concerned, either they will have to buy more from us or we shall have to buy less from them, because we still have an unfavourable balance of trade. That is exactly the situation in which the British

find themselves. It does not make any difference whether you are trying to bring about convertibility of currency or the establishment of an international currency; until there is co-operation you cannot solve the problem.
The Minister of Agriculture has pointed out that the reason we have fallen down on some of our former contracts with Britain is that we are consuming more in Canada. I do not believe anyone could criticize the government for that. I believe the best market for our products is the home market. If the reason for the reduction in imports is the consumption of more in this country, I would not criticize the government except to the extent that our production might have been expanded in order to take care of the increased demand. There is one danger though, and it is this: if we try to consume the greater part of our agricultural production at home, we may, as a result, lose our markets abroad. Then I suppose in future the prices at which goods were sold in Canada would be determined by the prices for the small amount exported abroad. That has usually been the attitude of governments in the past. If the price of the commodity exported abroad sets the price for the commodity we consume at home, then to the extent that we lose markets the difficulty will increase.
For this reason I am hoping the government will establish the Agricultural Prices Support Act on a sound basis. I know I am out of order in discussing that, but a resolution will be coming up next year to terminate that act. I looked upon it as permanent legislation. The minister has said there is no reason why it could not continue indefinitely. Now it seems an end is to be put to the life of that act. I believe that will be a definite breach of faith with the farmers of this country. As a result of certain sacrifices they have made in the past, they were guaranteed stabilization in the future, and not just for four years. I regret the appearance of that resolution on the order paper, and I hope that by the time it is brought down it will be in different shape.

May I make one comment about the last remark of the member for Acadia? He believes the British are not altogether to blame, and I should like to call his attention to the fact that, so far as I am aware-I may be wrong in this-it is only food products that are being declared surplus in the United States, as related to the provision of Marshall funds. This creates a difficulty in connection with food products that is not felt in connection with some other products. I do not blame the British for that; I do not blame anyone in particular. It is a fact, however. On behalf of our American

friends we have to say that although they did have 26 million acres more in wheat last year than they felt they ought to have, they did not declare wheat surplus in the sense in which it could have been declared surplus under the Marshall plan. Provision was made to help finance the sale of our wheat in Britain, and that is one of our important products. It has created some difficulties for us in connection with other products, and makes contracts of the type we have been making rather difficult.

All I can say is that the statement made by the minister this morning, along with the speech made in Brantford, to which I had the pleasure of listening, constitute the most important statement made by any member of this government in many years. I can assure the minister that I have a copy of the Brantford Expositor which carried his speech in detail. The only difference is that the Brantford Expositor has the headline, "British barrier to Canada's foods."
I have warned the minister and the members of this house on many occasions during the last two or three years as to what might take place. On one occasion in 1946 the minister took me to task for even suggesting that the British would not fulfil any of their agreements, whether they were by word of mouth or by signed contract. This morning the minister tells us that the United Kingdom in 1946 was trying to buy all our surplus farm products. Then he comes along and says that the situation now is actually reversed; that the United Kingdom is trying to drive all our farm products off their market. The statement made by the minister then, and by many other members of the government, that Britain had no dollars with which to buy our food, apparently has not been true.
Surely neither the minister nor anyone else in the House of Commons or in this country would expect that Britain would take only our surpluses of food products. Unless we can assure a stable market to Great Britain or any other country to whom we expect to sell our products, certainly we cannot expect to have that market. That is the thing that I have said was the trouble during the past two or three years. I have repeated it in this chamber on several occasions. I so stated when the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were being discussed the other night, and I repeat it now. It is not only a case of the dollar shortage; it is not a case of their wanting to see our products off the British market; it is the effect of this government's lack of foresight in not maintaining production and not
Supply-Agriculture
fulfilling the contracts which we had with Great Britain, and allowing production to go down to such a level that we could not supply the food products that Great Britain wanted. She was therefore forced to go elsewhere to buy the food that she required to feed her people.
It would be interesting if the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other night had put on the record the figures I asked for, or if the Minister of Agriculture would now put on the record figures with respect to the value of food products we have sent to Great Britain since the beginning of the war, the amount of the contract, and the amount we sent each year from 1942 or 1943 up to the present year. Those figures would be most interesting. I think all hon. members would agree that never since 1944-or it might have been 1944-45-have we filled a British contract, with the exception, probably, of that for eggs, and for cheese this year. The quantity of cheese this year, however, is the lowest quantity we have ever sent to Great Britain in the last fifty years.
The attitude now taken by the Minister of Agriculture is apparently very different from that taken in 1946, when both he and the then minister of trade and commerce assured us, and assured the farmers all across Canada, that if we supplied food to Great Britain at prices far less than world prices during those years, we could be assured of a future market at a reasonable level in the United Kingdom. That was the statement made on several occasions in this chamber by the minister.
I still believe that, but it may not be next year-in the future.

If it is not next year, it is not very satisfactory, is it? If we are going to cut out the odd year, what good is it?- because the very year we do not get these markets is the very year we are going to have a surplus in this country. Whether the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce believes it or not, there is a food surplus in this country today; whether they call it a surplus over domestic requirements, an unsold surplus, or whatever they wish to term it, there is still a surplus. We were all happy, as I have said, to supply Great Britain at that time; the farmers of this country never asked for all the traffic would bear with regard to the price of food; they were doing it partly on a patriotic basis and partly on a basis of maintaining those markets with Great Britain in future years. The thing the farmers across this country are fearful of now is that, having sold these things for less than the world price, they are

Supply-Agriculture
to be expected to take the low prices in the post-war era; and that is what they have been worrying about for the last number of years. This government always assured us, through the federation of agriculture and through the House of Commons, that they were going to stabilize farm prices; and one means they were going to use to do that was through the Agricultural Products Act and the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
I see that on the order paper there are two resolutions having to do with prices support acts. I grant you they are not to be taken up this session, but it is obvious that the government has in mind taking out section 9, the operative section, of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Now that this whole market situation has fallen down over his ears, the Minister of Agriculture is looking for a scapegoat.
Oh, no.
Mr. Chairman, it is fairly obvious that he is looking for somebody to blame for the situation.
I am not blaming anybody.
The minister is not blaming anybody?
No.
Yet he says-

Why should I blame anybody? Two days ago I hunted all over to find a few bottles of milk or a few cans of milk and a few pounds of something else to sell to a group of people who were here to buy these things, and I could not find them. Why should I be blaming anybody for the condition? We have no surpluses of these food products. The food is all gone. I have no complaint to make about that. That is what we grow it for. We grow it in order that somebody may consume it.

I think it is fairly obvious from this newspaper report-the minister himself read it over this morning-and from the newspaper reports which have appeared in many papers since that Brantford speech, that he is blaming the government of Great Britain now for not wanting our food.

I do not withdraw that, either. The government of Great Britain does not want our food; but in spite of the fact that the government of Great Britain does not want our food, we have sold it all. I do not think it is going to be a good condition for the future. I think we must have the British markets in which to sell our foods some years ahead; I do not know just when, but some years from now.
What is the government doing to get those markets?
Trying to keep our contract with them.
The minister says there are no food surpluses. I wonder if the apple growers across this country will believe that. I wonder if the milk producers across this country will believe that.
I think even the apple growers will believe that.

That there are no surpluses of apples? I am sorry, but I am afraid the minister is being extremely optimistic. Here is a statement in the Ottawa Journal of November 9, for instance, which is headed: "Processed milk and butter surpluses proving problem". Has that been sold?
When was that?
November 9.
That may be. But they are not here this week. They are gone.
Is the minister trying to tell me that 56,600,000 pounds of powdered milk and condensed milk were sold since November 9?

Yes. I am trying to tell the hon. member that within the last week I have been trying to find powdered milk, canned milk and milk of any kind to sell to anybody, and could not find it. If there was 56 million pounds here then, it is not here now, begging for a market.
I wonder if the hon. member for Leeds will believe that. He talked about the supplies stored in church basements.
Yes, I think he will. He had a newspaper here the other day. He was going to quote it. I do not think he is here now, but he will have it here and quote it to you after a while.

The minister still says there are no surpluses in Canada. He has all the figures. He has all the departmental officials in front of him. I have talked to some of these officials within the last week, and they tell me a different story. I do not know whom we can believe, if we cannot take the figures in the Trade and Commerce booklet, and if we cannot take the figures which are given to the press, obviously from the department.

I have here a list of products which was handed to me the other day by people who wished to buy them. It includes skim milk powder to the extent of 920 tons,

I believe it is; whole milk powder, 600 tons; yellow cheese, 1,200 tons; fillets of fish, 1,440 tons; canned fish, 900,000 tons; egg powder, 480,000 tons; canned vegetables, 7,200 tons. Then it deals with grits, barley and maize, frozen wheat and buckwheat, and canned milk. I went right down that list with the branches that are presumed to have them, and was told that we have none of those surpluses left whatsoever under our control. The only way they could buy these products is to go out and buy them in competition with other countries at prices they are prepared to pay for it.
What prices were offered for those materials?
I have them here, but it is a lengthy list.
They are low, I imagine, as compared with previous prices.
The price is lower than they were prepared to offer for some.
The price we were asking is lower than they were prepared to pay.
The price, as I understand, at which they could be bought is nine or ten or eleven cents on the first one, thirty-four on the second one, and so on.
What products are they?
Skim milk and whole milk powder.

It is characteristic, because the minister told us this morning that England offered us more for our beef than this government wanted to charge them for it, just to maintain price control and to maintain the low cost of living. So that we could expect the government to sell our products for less than they could get for them.
But we had price control then, and we have not now.

Well, this is still the most discouraging statement made in this House of Commons for many years. I am sure the farmers of Canada will take it as a very strange Christmas present to come from the government.
Oh, oh.
Everyone on that side of the house seems to treat it as a joke.
It is not a joke.

Certainly it is not a joke. It is a different story now from the one that was told prior to the election. The minister says he told the same story. One newspaper after another quoted what the Minister of

Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture said. The London Free Press of October 21, 1949, carries a headline, "Trade protection key Canadian policy-Howe" and
states:
Need of Adjustments
"Ours is a healthy, prosperous, well-balanced and in fact a booming economy," he added. While there were indications that 1950 would be a favourable year in exports, there would need to be some adjustments.
These adjustments may see the exports figures not as "impressive" as those attained in 1949.
"Not as impressive". Of course we are not going to sell as much. He says they are not as impressive as they were in 1949. The report goes on:
High domestic demand, nevertheless, would cushion the effect of any adjustments. The domestic demand already has been able to fill the gap created by export markets restrictions.
Then follows the heading "domestic markets strong," and the minister goes on to tell how the domestic market is strong. That is true of many things. But is the domestic market enough to take all those surpluses which we will have?
I have here a telegram from the hog producers of my own riding, and they say they are discouraged about the situation at present.
They say they want a contract with Britain.
Yes.
I got the telegram, too.
They want a contract for more than one year, and they want to know what the contract price is.
And the British will not sign one for more than one year.
That is something which this government has never given.
The British will not sign a contract for more than one year, and if they have their way they will not sign one at all; but I think they are going to sign one.

It seems strange that they will sign contracts with other nations, even behind the iron curtain, for terms of two or three years-yes, fifteen years. They sign those contracts; I do not know why they will not sign similar contracts with us. Apparently the department is not prepared to sign those contracts for more than one year.

No; we have been trying to sign them for four or five years, but they have refused to sign them, either during the war or since, for more than two years

Supply-A griculture
on anything but wheat. We heard a lot of criticism from hon. members on the other side of the house for signing one on wheat for four years.

Possibly they have refused, when contracts have been for anywhere from 200 million to 300 million bushels and they were sent only half of it. You cannot expect to sign a contract for four or five years under that condition.
Probably not, but the hon. member's statement is not correct.
What is wrong with it?

My hon. friend stated the position correctly himself at the beginning of his remarks, when he was sticking to the record. Our production went up until 1944. We did fill the contract, and more than filled it every year. Of course the reason why we did not fill it after that is that the British came here in 1944 and said they would not sign a contract for a higher amount. They would only take 450 million pounds after that, where they had been taking 700 million. When they wanted to write it into a contract we refused to write it into a one-year contract, and finally agreed to write 900 million pounds into a two-year contract. That is the way it turned out. That is the way it went down, and we allowed it to go down deliberately because the market was not there.

There is a big difference between 450 million pounds a year and 56 million or 55 million, as we have it this year. But of course the minister will find some excuse for lowering of production; naturally he will not blame the government. I still say it was lack of foresight on the part of the government. Taking the ceiling price off feed grains was one thing. In 1947 the price of little pigs went down to nothing, absolutely nothing. They were killed and thrown on manure piles in some parts of Canada.
Farmers do not do that.
Some of the people here who claim to know so much about farmers have been away from farming so long they have lost track of it.
I go back three or four times a year.
Apparently the hon. member does not go out behind the barn; you stay in the house.

The only little pigs that were ever thrown out behind the barn of any farm I was ever on-and I have been on them

from one end of Canada to the other-were those that died a natural death, in spite of all the farmer could do. He did not kill them.

I told a story in the fall of 1947 about a chap who was trying to sell pigs and who put a sign on his trailer which he left outside stating that anybody who would take them was welcome to them. When he came back there were twice as many pigs in the trailer as when he went in.
But that never happened.

Do you say it never
happened?
No; it is a good story, but it did not happen.

The Rural Co-operator of Toronto, Ontario, states in a headline on October 11, "Gardiner says market not lost if nothing to sell." That was the kind of statement that was made prior to the election. The last statement made at Brantford and which was directed to the farmers was that the farmers across Canada would do just as well to sow what they wanted of the products they could make the most money with and then everything would be all right. That was quite an optimistic statement coming on the heels of the statement the minister made previously with regard to the British export market.
Everyone knows that we must depend upon our export markets. As I have said on previous occasions, we cannot look to the United States to provide markets for our agricultural products. The United States is a competitor and the year we might have a surplus of products, the United States would have a surplus of the same products and would not permit ours to be shipped there.
While the minister did not name the product, I have no doubt he was referring to cheese that is being shipped by the United States to Great Britain, and to the fact that this government had not permitted cheese to be sent from this country to the United States. Would we expect them to take it when they were exporting to the United Kingdom?

Let me read to the hon. member the report he is looking for and then he can find the answers he wants. Here is what is said in the Brantford paper:
The minister said: We can produce more cheese now and enter into a larger contract with the United Kingdom next year.
Then the report continues:
In conclusion he advised farmers: "Use your farm the way you have used it in the past. Produce as much as you feel you want to produce,

and I am sure that we will maintain good relations between the farming community and the industrial community."

That statement could have been made 25 or 30 years ago. Another statement made at Brantford by the minister was that the United States was going to reduce its wheat acreage by some 26 million acres. Are we going to continue to expect the United States to carry the agriculture of this country? It has been ECA dollars that have paid for the wheat and many other of our products that have been sent to Great Britain in the last couple of years and now the minister states that the United States are going to reduce their wheat acreage.
The hon. member should tell the committee what he said at the Brantford meeting.

Sometimes one says the things one is expected to say on such an occasion, but I do not always believe them. In thanking a speaker who had come that distance it would only be common decency and courtesy for me not to disagree with the statements he made on that occasion. I do not think that, with the minister coming into my home riding, I would be expected to do that.
1 showed that much courtesy to the minister, out I am sure I am not called upon to show *he same courtesy here in the House of Commons that was shown to him in Brant-:ord.
You showed much more lourtesy than there was any occasion for. Does the hon. member want to repeat what le said?
I do not need to repeat it.

Has the minister received any requests from the department of agriculture in New Brunswick or from anyone else in that province to support the price of potatoes? This season we have had the largest potato crop ever produced, and on December 1 there was the largest amount in storage ever known. the government of Prince Edward Island to put on a support price. Up to the present time it has not been done.

On September 30 I spoke before the committee, and my remarks were of a very gloomy nature concerning the future of the evaporated milk industry. I was referring entirely to a local situation, and at that time my figures were absolutely correct. Since then a very different picture has presented itself to the industry. I am only speaking now of evaporated milk. The situation that had developed has resolved itself, and I can say confidently that today the industry is in a substantially better position. In fact exports of evaporated milk have gone ahead in an extraordinary manner.
That was because of the by-election.

The by-election had nothing to do with milk. The markets that have been found are chiefly in Europe. I want to commend both the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture for their unfailing efforts to develop the markets of Canada, harbingers of gloom on the other side and reports to the contrary notwithstanding.
You should have a talk with them before you make another speech.

I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture one question. As the result of the remarkable statement he made this morning, is he now in a position to admit that he accepted too low a price for the products he sold in the British market during the war?

Mr. Chairman, in the first place I do not admit that the statement was remarkable. In the second place I do not admit that, so far as any of the products we have been discussing are concerned, we accepted a low price from the British for them. An examination of the markets now will indicate that we are asking a higher price than most other people are getting in the British market.

I do not think that answers the question. During the war years you sold our agricultural products to Great Britain for less than you could have sold them on any other market with the understanding that we were to continue to have the British market after the war. I should like you tc admit that one thing.
I will not admit any such statement.
No, you will not admit it, bu' you should.

I should not admit it. Then were only a few months during whicl Canadian farmers could have sold their foot products at higher prices than they wen sold. Mr. Chairman, the department whose estimates have just been completed has some relationship to the discussion now before us, because of the similarity of the subject matter in so far as a number of the items are concerned. One of the points I should like to emphasize particularly is something that was said by the Minister of Agriculture in a speech he made last year in London. It was delivered to the chamber of commerce on December 17, 1948, and I am referring to it because of what seems to me to keep recurring in any discussion of trade, or of our business activities of any kind.
After reviewing the situation with which he thought Canada was confronted at the time, the Minister of Agriculture said this- I suggest that it has a great deal to do with the whole trade and commerce situation with which we are confronted.
I am convinced that the world is not in any state of mind where it can expect to agree that the manipulation of any system or systems of currency is going to be allowed1 to interfere with the will of those who have empty stomachs, when it is preventing surpluses of food to get to them. It might be a good thing for everybody if they closed down United Nations' meetings long enough to permit of the United Kingdom and United States experts getting together and settling some basis upon which dollars and sterling can be converted, to allow nations like Canada to produce food to feed tne starving millions, and distribute it.
In those words, I believe the Minister of Agriculture has pointed to the greatest need of this period, if we are not to find barriers in the way of trade which will cause difficulties, no matter how optimistic the predictions might be. I repeat the suggestion that was presented earlier in	this	session,	that thegovernment of Canada should not wait for action to be taken by the government of the United Kingdom and the United States but that it should itself take the initiative in seeking to find some	way	in	which Canadacan trade with the	sterling	area.	If thisproblem is tackled, I believe that we may find the solution for the broader problem; because if we can	find	a	way	to trade
effectively with Britain, then at the same time we shall have found a way to trade effectively with the rest of the sterling area; and if we find that solution, we shall have found a solution for the broader problem, which will be to the advantage of the United States as well as Canada.
There is a reason why Canada is in a better position to make proposals which might solve this problem than is the United States. Even with the full recognition of the great service that the government of the United States has done to all mankind by the financial resources which that government has

made available to the nations of Europe and to other nations throughout the world during the period of recovery, there is still some measure of reluctance to disregard the possibility that the financial power of the United States may be exercised in a way that might reduce the complete freedom of action of some of the other nations. That suggestion can never be made with regard to Canada. Fortunately we are not large enough, from the financial point of view, to be in a position to threaten the economic position of any other country. Nevertheless, we are large enough, and financially strong enough, to enter into discussions which might form a pattern for other nations in the sterling area and ultimately for a solution of this broad problem.
I am not going to quote in detail the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce which gave an optimistic picture that seems to be so greatly in conflict with the picture given to us this morning by the Minister of Agriculture, as to the immediate prospects for the sale of our agricultural commodities. Nevertheless, the speech that he made here on December 1 can be summed up by saying that it was an optimistic speech, and all of us will hope that optimism may be the spirit in which all our problems will be tackled; but it was a speech in which the optimism that was expressed refused to admit the many suggestions that were made that there was a real reason for concern for the immediate trade picture.
It is not necessary for me either at this time to quote the statements made by the leading representatives of the Canadian chambers of commerce, of the exporters' association or of other organizations whose business it is to stimulate the trading activities of this country. Everyone has read them. Everyone knows that there is being expressed, by those whose personal business is export trade, a feeling of concern which is not in keeping with the statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his speech of December 1.
Then we also have a recent speech by the Minister of Finance in which the word "crisis" appeared in the heading above the speech; and there again we have the difference-

speechtext: It is a great newspaper.

I felt sure that the minister would agree with that. We have the constant appearance of the word "crisis" and the word "threat", and now today we have the statement by the Minister of Agriculture that we are being squeezed out of the British market.
It is not necessary to debate what the interpretation of any of these statements or speeches really should be. If confirmation were needed of the real concern which has been felt for some time by Canadians about the future of our export trade, particularly in the line of agricultural products, that doubt was removed this morning by the speech of the Minister of Agriculture. The question ' before us is not whether there is danger to our export trade, but whether it is possible to find any way to meet the situation with which we are confronted today.
It may well be that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not the one to deal with financial problems as such; but again may I point out the recurrence, in speech after speech of those in the government ranks and in statements prepared by government agencies, of expressions of the need for finding some solution to the present problem presented by the inconvertibility of sterling and dollars.
This is not a problem that we can sit back and wait to see solved. Our position is not the same as that of the United States. This is a special problem of our own. With the importance of overseas export markets-and I underline those words "overseas export markets"-it is essential to the future prosperity of this country that we should not wait for any other nation to find a solution of that problem which now confronts us and which presents these immediate dangers, as was clearly expressed by the Minister of Agriculture today. Shipping, shipbuilding, the export of our industrial products and of our agricultural products, all are related to a solution of this difficulty, as has already been stated in this chamber and as has appeared in reports of such government agencies as the maritime commission. Therefore, without seeking to go back and balance one interpretation against another of the things that have been said in the past, I urge with all the earnestness that I believe the present situation demands that in meeting problems of trade and commerce, particularly export trade, Canada take the initiative in trying to find

Supply-Trade and Commerce a solution to the very difficulty which was so clearly stated by the Minister of Agriculture in London last December.
As he said at that time, I do not think the people of Canada or the people of the rest of the world are nearly so concerned about the details of exchange problems as they are about finding a way in which we can trade, and finding a way in which there can be convertibility of money, no matter what the unit of money may be. We do not want to see this world divided into three economic areas, one behind the iron curtain, one in the sterling area and one in the dollar area. I would hope that, without any regard to past statements or past points of view, Canada for the particular purpose of holding our trade and expanding it in the years ahead will take the initiative in seeking a solution of this very grave problem.

Can the minister tell the committee what policy is in effect as to inventions which were taken over by the government? Inventions are handled by the national research council under a policy that has been established within the last twelve months. My hon. friend now asks me what the policy is. I am sending for the officer who can give me that accurately. At the moment I would hesitate to tell the hon. member what the policy is.

I should like to ask the minister whether officials of this department are allowed to take out patents for inventions they discover while working for the research council, then resign from the research council and go out and make millions of dollars out of the invention.

No, the policy definitely does not permit that. Generally speaking, anything that is invented during employment by the government, that is, by a man who is receiving a full-time salary from the government, is the property of the government. What I was going to ask my officer was whether there is any provision for participation by the man. I now am told there is a provision under the policy of national research council that if a patent is sold by the council, the man whose work made the patent possible for the government is entitled to a return of 5 per cent of the gross receipts from the sale.
The official I have in mind patented this article, resigned from the council, and then went out and made millions of dollars.
I suggest to my hon. friend that was not an official of the national research council. I think he was an official of mines and resources, was he not?

Supply-Trade and Commerce
If we are thinking of the same man, I think he was.
He was a full-time employee . of the national research council. Let us put it that way.
The policy I have just enunciated was put into effect on the first of January, 1949, and applies to inventions from that time on.

The position during the war was that all inventions by men in the armed services or men employed on government payrolls, directly or indirectly, had no participation in the rewards from their inventions. The staffs were large; it was too difficult to sort out who was responsible for what. As I say, at the beginning of 1949 a new policy was instituted, which is the government policy for all departments. I should like to ask the minister to give us as frank and detached an opinion about the work of the national research council as he did about the trade fair. Supply-Trade and Commerce The employees of the board of grain commissioners, and particularly those stationed in the railway yards in Winnipeg, were kept on a 5| or six-day week. I should like to ask the minister about two buildings, one of which is known as the Alvin estates building and the other as the Begg building, both in Vancouver, and also about the proposed new post office building for Vancouver.
I would refer first to the Alvin estates building, where the office of the unemployment insurance commission is located. From whom was the building purchased and at what cost?

speechtext: The cost will be $862,155. Additional work had to be done to the extent of $200,950. The estimated cost will be $1,100,000. This will be a federal building, and we are going to purchase it.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Alvin estates. I do not know just who they are.

speechtext: My deputy tells me that is so.
Is this the total amount to be involved, or is something more than this $1,100,000 to be paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am told this is the whole amount for the purchase of the building. At one time we had no space for the unemployment insurance commission. We tried to secure the national defence building, but did not succeed. Then we entered into a contract with these people to put up a building at a stated rental per year, and we have the option of purchasing it after one year's occupancy.	We have decided to
purchase the building.
Will the minister table the agreement between his department and this construction firm?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes. That would be the order in council passed when we undertook to buy the building. There was a clause giving us the option of purchasing.
Will the minister table in the house a copy of that agreement?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If we do not prorogue, we shall; if we do prorogue I shall have a copy of the order in council sent to my hon. friend.

I bring this point up because I think this is a very wasteful way of constructing a building. I understand the picture is this: Certain parties who are pretty friendly to the government got the property first. I believe the price paid originally for the property-that is, the land-was about $45,000. I am not clear whether they bought the land outright or just took it on option. Then this company, the Alvin Estates Limited, was formed; and Allan and Viner, who are the contractors, I believe are two of the men in the company.
Then they transferred the property to the company. Debentures were issued to the amount of $650,000. I think those debentures are held by the same individuals who had the company incorporated. At first they had a very good lease from the department containing the right of the department to purchase. Then the department exercised that right to purchase the building at a total cost, we are told, of $1,100,000.
It is hard to understand why the department did not simply buy the land and erect a building, calling for tenders in the ordinary way instead of going around the corner and dealing with friends, as would appear to have been done in this case. I am afraid the result is that this building has cost a great deal more than if it had been constructed in the ordinary way and if competitive bids had been called. Can the minister say why this roundabout policy has been followed?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The explanation I have is that at one time the unemployment insurance branch lacked space in Vancouver. We sent out our Mr. Mills to make an inquiry into conditions and he could not find any space in Vancouver at that time. To have put up a first-class building, such as we would have put up in Vancouver, would have taken more time than the securing of this building. A note I have here states that no office buildings for rentals have been constructed in Vancouver since 1939, and that in view of the extremely rapid growth of the city there is no available office space in the locality In March of 1948 Alvin Estates Limited offered to construct a four-storey building and to rent

it to the department on a ten-year lease at a rental of $96,000 a year. There was no available space in the city when this deal was made. We were pressed by the unemployment insurance people who required space for their administration. The offer also included the option to purchase by the department after one year's occupancy. We think it is cheaper to become the owners of the building than to continue to pay rent. During the war and for the last two or three years we have been hard-pressed for building space. In many cases time was of the essence. I am thinking of one case that was settled only two weeks ago at the request of some hon. members.
Why does not the department purchase land through a real estate firm in the way that an ordinary company would instead of making these payments to friends of the government who have property?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In normal times I agree that what the hon. member is saying would be the correct thing, that if we had time it would be better to acquire these buildings. The hon. gentleman has been here a long time and he knows that during the war I did not have any estimates for the construction of buildings. For a number of years after the war we were told that we should let materials and labour go for private housing which was in short supply.
This deal was made last year. Is the department still carrying on in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In certain cases; in extraordinary cases. The unemployment insurance had to vacate the old Vancouver hotel and we tried to get space in the armouries from national defence but they would not release it. We had a man stationed there who was trying to make some sort of a deal so that unemployment insurance would not be out on the street. I agree that except in these extraordinary circumstances we should construct buildings.
I do not think the department gets space any more quickly with a deal of this kind than by buying the land and building.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have another case in Vancouver where we have been trying to get a site for three years.
What it all adds up to is that some friend of the government gets a nice bit of money out of this deal. It is a most inefficient way of handling the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would not admit that. A man coming to Ottawa may find it most

I want to say a word on this item. We want a bridge. I think the minister has heard about this bridge before. We want that bridge across the Ottawa river, about four miles east of Pembroke. This is a very modest request, but the matter is urgent; it has been urgent and necessary for the last fifty years, but still the bridge has not been built. I know the plans and blueprints are all ready, and I know the minister will tell me that he must wait until either Quebec or Ontario requests that the bridge be built. I am going to make a suggestion, and I hope the minister will listen. If the provinces hesitate or refuse to approach the federal government, will the minister not consider approaching the public works departments of either Ontario or Quebec, or both, asking them to meet here to consult with respect to this bridge?
The matter is urgent for many reasons. It is important in connection with the tourist traffic. It is important with respect to the health of our people, who for weeks in the spring and fall of the year cannot get to hospital without going four or five hundred miles out of their way, because of blocked roads. We want that bridge and we want it soon; we should have had it years ago. If the minister would just take the bit in his teeth and request the co-operation of Ontario and Quebec we probably would get the bridge. We would like it to be built at once; it is badly needed, and under any circumstances, give us a bridge.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after what has been said by the two hon. members who have just spoken, I hesitate to deal with a technical matter at this time, but at least the point I intend to raise will not take long to discuss. In fact it may make it possible for the Minister of Finance to clear up a point. I want to make it clear that I do not raise the question in any critical spirit, nor am I opposed to the expenditure of the money involved.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister will remember that a few days ago, when we were discussing the bill to provide salaries for the new ministers I asked whether provision would be made for the usual car allowances that minister's enjoy. The Prime Minister told me that that point had presented itself to him but he had been advised that it would be covered in the estimates of 1931. I made the natural response that I would like to look into it for myself, and I have done that. I have here Appropriation Act No. 5, 1931, which is chapter 61 of the statutes of that year. Item 352 reads:
352. To provide for payment annually from the consolidated revenue fund of the sum of $2,000 to each minister of the crown charged with the administration of a department, the solicitor general, and the leader of the opposition, and the sum of $1,000 each to the Speaker of the Senate and the Speaker of the House of Commons, in lieu of motor cars and their maintenance, including chauffeurs, the acceptance of such sums not to vacate their respective seats in parliament; and to authorize the governor in council to appoint any person now employed in the public service as a chauffeur of a passenger automobile at Ottawa, whose position is abolished, to a vacant position in the public service, provided such chauffeur has been continuously employed as such for at least two years and that the appointment will be made at no higher remuneration than he is now receiving, $42,000.
Actually it was not necessary to read the whole item, but I thought I should, lest after reading only the pertinent part someone should ask that I read it all. As I see it, the point is quite clear. In 1931 the House of Commons passed an Appropriation Act which provided for a sum of $42,000. It is clear from the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, which was amended in that same year, that no sum can be paid out in excess of the amount appropriated by parliament. No matter how that item may be worded, I cannot see how an amount in excess of $42,000 can be paid.
I recognize that the word "annually" appears in the item, which might seem to give permission to pay that sum annually; but is it not also essential that the total amount paid shall not exceed $42,000? The fact is that

most of that $42,000 was paid in that fiscal year. I looked up the public accounts and found that some $30,000 odd was paid. Section 32, subsection 1, of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, reads:
Balances of appropriations which remain unexpended at the end of a fiscal year shall lapse and be written off.
In other words it would seem to me that whatever was left of that $42,000 as the end of 1931-32 would lapse.
May I call attention to one or two other sections in the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. Section 22, subsection 1, reads:
Subject to the provisions of subsection two of this section, no issue of public moneys out of the consolidated revenue fund shall be made except under the authority of parliament.
Section 23 reads:
All estimates of expenditures submitted to parliament shall be for the services coming in course of payment during the fiscal year.
Section 24 is a long section, but it ends with these words:
-not exceeding the amount of the sum so voted or granted.
I come back to the point I made. All I am arguing for is that this $2,000 should be properly provided for by a statute, because it seems to me that once the 1931-32 fiscal year ended, whatever part of that money had not been spent would lapse. I do not see how the government can go on making payments year after year on the strength of the $42,000 voted in 1931.
The item which I referred to is to be found in schedule A attached to chapter 61 of the statutes of 1931; and it is stated that the items in that schedule are based on the main estimates for that year. That act provides that the amounts expended under the terms of schedule A shall not exceed a certain rather large figure.
As the minister knows, there are frequent occasions on which it becomes necessary to get authorization from parliament to make commitments to be expended in future years. Last night we had a case in the Department of Mines and Resources about which I inquired. I confess that I knew the answer before I asked my question, but I wanted to get it on the record. The Minister of Mines and Resources made it quite clear that what the government was asking for was authority to commit the government to a future expenditure, but he answered me, I think correctly, that a vote would have to appear in the estimates for each year in which money was paid to carry out such a commitment. The same thing shows up in the estimates of the Department of National Defence, where a number of commitments are made for future

years, and lor which authorization is sought in the current fiscal year. It is always clearly understood that when the time comes to pay the amount committed, it will require a vote of parliament.
I have no thought that I am raising a problem which has not presented itself to others in times past. The Prime Minister indicated that it had presented itself to him this year. I have gone into this as carefully as I can, but I stand to be educated on the point by the Minister of Finance. Nevertheless, it does seem to me that he is going to have a hard job explaining that you can continue to pay out $40,000 a year on the strength of an item voted in 1931. Remember that on that occasion the vote was for a sum of money not to exceed $42,000.
Is this the correct way to do it? Should it not be done by statute? Is it proper to have these items marked "statutory" in the estimates when there is no statute covering them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend pursues these purely legal questions I always follow his legal arguments with a great deal of interest. Perhaps it is not necessary for me to say that the Minister of Finance has received a formal opinion from the deputy minister of justice that this is what is known as a continuing vote. From year to year the estimates are filled with items of this kind, including a number of pension items, which are voted once in an appropriation bill but which continue as a statutory charge. I am sure if it were not so late in the session-it may happen even now-there would be many members of the house who would rise to support me. In fact I hope two or three of them will do so, in order that the minister may know that I am not "a voice crying in the wilderness". I feel that the answers which were given in the last parliament were not good enough. To put it briefly, if a province having the financial difficulties of Newfoundland can do that well; if it can be done in Saskatchewan and the United Kingdom, surely this federal government can do it, and I urge action on this important matter without further delay.

I should like to join in the plea made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. There is really very little that can be added to the statement he has made, but I should like to point out to the minister that when these civil servants were making their payments they believed that their retirement allowances would be sufficient for them to be able to carry on. Because of the increase in the cost of living, some of them, particularly those in the lower brackets, are now in a very difficult position. We have a large number of retired federal civil servants in British Columbia, and personally I know of a good many cases in which there is considerable suffering because of the inadequacy of the pension. It seems to me that Canada might very well take the lead in meeting this situation. Certain industries have made some provision in this regard and

I suggest that the minister give further consideration to the plea that something be done for retired civil servants.

I think what has already been said points to the necessity for a re-examination of the whole basis of the pension schemes. There is no questioning the fact that actuarially the whole basis of the contributory pension scheme is wrong from the point of view of the decreasing value of money. You cannot say today, nor can any actuary, what will be the value of a man's pension forty years from now. When we ask for a contribution of a certain percentage of a man's salary and say that in twenty or thirty years his pension will be so much, we are sticking our heads in the sand, because we all know that the inexorable trend is for money to diminish in value, since prices are constantly going up. It seems to me we shall have to call for a complete re-examination of the whole basis of our pension program if we are to give our civil servants a fair deal; and I ask that this be done.

Items 938 and 939 recall a statement by the Minister of Finance a couple of weeks ago concerning grants to municipalities, in lieu of taxes on property owned by the crown in the right of the dominion, or agencies of the crown in the right of the dominion. I do not propose to go into that very confusing statement at great length, but the minister has referred to it since as being a clear statement. There are not many people who have commented upon the statement, editorially or otherwise, who have found it clear. Practically every municipality in Canada has found it a most disappointing statement of policy.
In the light of statements that have been made from time to time by the government, it had been hoped that the government did appreciate that the time had come when it ought, in all fairness, to make to municipalities, in lieu of taxes, grants that would at least be a reasonable approach to the amount that federally-owned properties would have borne in taxes had they been owned by private individuals. The statement which the minister made seems to be based upon the assumption that only the municipalities having more than an average of federally owned property should qualify for any federal assistance whatever. With respect, I believe that is an entirely unfair decision. Here is a government that is amply provided with revenues and which, so far as its taxing powers are concerned, has unlimited sources of revenue. The municipalities with which we are concerned are all suffering seriously from limited sources of revenue and rising costs of services; and, I may say, Mr. Chairman, an extremely unfair burden of services has been cast upon them. There is hardly a municipality in this country, certainly among the larger municipalities, which in recent times has not been ground between the upper and nether millstones of limited sources of revenue and rising costs of services. Formerly, these were regarded as the municipality's responsibility, but today enlightened opinion regards many of them as the proper responsibility of the federal government.
In connection with the recent amendment to the housing act, the minister of reconstruction gave a clear undertaking that, for all the houses that would be owned by the federal authorities or constructed under the new legislation, payments would be made to the municipalities in lieu of taxes equal to

the amount of taxes which those properties would have borne had they been in private hands. That was a fair enough example for the Minister of Finance to follow.

It is expected to continue providing services. The whole situation is lamentably unfair, Mr. Chairman. I say to the minister that before another session comes around I hope he will have the courage and determination to take the situation in hand and see that fair play and justice are extended to all municipalities which have federally-owned property within their borders.
