speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I was about to express my protest against the formula that the minister has produced with respect to the matter of the federal government paying something to municipalities in lieu of taxes on crown properties. The day the minister announced his formula it seemed to me that, in those earlier stages of what he had to say, it sounded good. I thought he was laying the basis, theoretically, for a formula that would be acceptable. It looked to me as though we would get some sort of sliding scale that, despite its discrimination against some places, would at least be defensible. But when he came down not with a sliding scale but with [DOT]one that cuts off abruptly, and provides no relief to a great many cities and municipalities of the country, I felt that it was most unfair and certainly did not solve the problem.
I can state my protest perhaps most readily by reading a few sentences from a letter which I received from the mayor of Winnipeg, Mr. Garnet Coulter, which I believe is in terms identical with those of letters received by each of the other members from the city of Winnipeg. The letter is dated December 6, 1949. I am not going to read all of it, but just a few selected sentences that drive home the point. I quote from Mayor Coulter's letter:
In October of this year I was one of a delegation from the executive committee-

That is the executive committee of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities.
-who waited on the Prime Minister when he told us that the government did have a plan under consideration which would be before the present session of the house, and we were all encouraged to believe that this issue was on its way to at least a partially fair solution.
The members of our city council were therefore very surprised and disappointed when the announcement of the details of the government proposal was made by Mr. Abbott. That proposal carries little or no benefit to any Canadian city, with the exception of two or three, of which group Winnipeg is not one. So the old situation still remains with our city gratuitously furnishing expensive services from which the government benefits.
I can assure you that a great deal of resentment has been created, not only here but in the other major cities of Canada, by the action of the government in purporting to deal with the situation and then having produced a formula which does not deal with it with any degree of adequacy.
Then I skip a few sentences in which the mayor tells me that the finance committee asked him to write to all four of the members for the city of Winnipeg, two of us being over here in this group and two on the government side, and then he goes on to say:
I was also requested to urge you, and the other members, to do anything possible to have the proposal revised so that at least some recognition of the moral right of the cities will be given.
My information is that since the proposal was announced by the government it has been scrutinized again by the executive committee and national advisory board of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, and that a protest is being forwarded to the cabinet, as well as a counter-suggestion, that the government should make payments in lieu of taxes to the extent that the government properties receive service benefits from the respective cities.
The letter has another paragraph and then it is signed:	"Yours very truly, Garnet
Coulter, mayor".
I have two or three questions to ask. First of all, I should like to ask the minister whether the protest and the countersuggestion referred to in Mayor Coulter's letter have been received and whether consideration has been given to such correspondence. My other question is this, and I ask it in the light of the discussion a few minutes ago about ministerial car allowances. Is the wording of this item such that it is a continuing item that does not have to be voted again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. In my public statement I announced that we put a single item in this year, and that a special statute would be introduced at the next session.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is fine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is in my statement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
So this is just for the current fiscal year. Will the minister tell me whether

this protest and counter-suggestion have been received since his statement was made and whether consideration has been given to them, in the light of the assurance that the mayors felt they had had from previous interviews?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not recall that particular protest. When the federation of mayors were here, in their brief they expressed some dissatisfaction with the formula as they understood it. Perhaps I might say at this point that there is not a great deal that I can add to the perhaps lengthy and complicated statement I made when I announced this policy, but here is the position. If federal property was distributed evenly throughout all the municipalities in Canada, obviously no taxes should be paid, since they are providing services, and the federal service would be distributed evenly throughout different municipalities. That is the basis upon which the exemption on taxation is contained in the British North America Act, and it is computed in every other way we have been able to find on a similar basis.
The justification for paying the tax to municipalities is that there is undue concentration of federal property and services in those municipalities. The basis of the proposed formula for the payment of general taxes is that, where there is an excess above what is established as a national average, then the taxes should be paid with respect to that excess, and that excess only.
It seems to me however that in the public comment respecting the outline of the proposed policy insufficient attention has been paid to the fact that in the case of crown corporations tax agreements will be made for the payment of fair sums in lieu of taxes, a procedure which has not been generally followed in the past. Secondly, all municipalities will receive payment for local improvement taxes, both current and arrears, if they have not been paid. That is something which has not been done in the past.
Thirdly, these transition payments will be made in any municipality where the federal government acquires property. It will pay the taxes for a period of three or five years, as the case may be, depending upon whether the municipality is one in receipt of the general grant or otherwise. Those are very substantial changes in the heretofore existing law.
I have only one further word to say, and that is that people should not jump to too hasty conclusions as to how this proposed formula will work out. It will require a
Supply-Finance
very considerable amount of additional work and time to get at the fair value of the different federal government-owned properties in the different municipalities, and to determine which municipalities are entitled to specific grants, and the extent of those grants.
The vote now before the committee is a purely interim vote. The primary purpose is to carry up to the end of the year the grant which has been paid to the city of Ottawa for a great many years. The other item of $300,000 is to provide for the setting up of a special grant in the treasury, to which I referred in my statement, and for the future possibly another grant which it may be necessary to make between January 1 and March 31, the end of the fiscal year.
One point I omitted to mention in connection with the new policy is that payment will be made in all cases for specific services in connection with federal property-services such as water, and all that sort of thing.

The minister has told us that we should not jump to hasty conclusions. I wish to associate myself with what was said by the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre in regard to this very ingenious but unconvincing procedure the minister has suggested. I should like to point out also that this is a piece of class legislation, because what the minister is doing is to favour people who are above, as against those who are below the average.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the last remark of the hon. member scarcely does credit to his very high intellectual attainments. Surely my hon. friend is not suggesting that every town in Canada which has a post office should be taxed on that post office. And I just refer to that as an example. Clearly a post office is providing a local service which the municipality needs and wants. Nearly every municipality has a post office, either rented or owned. That is an obvious case.
To say that we are benefiting those who are over the average and discriminating against those who are under is exactly the reverse of the principle which should be operative, and exactly the reverse of the actual fact.

I have not taken up much time, and I should like to ask the minister a question as to how this act works out. In my riding there is a large army camp and a large airport, of which I am very proud. The preliminary talk was such that the municipalities thought they were getting

Supply-Finance
something out of it. My understanding now is that municipalities such as Chilliwack will get nothing out of it. I would ask, as the Minister of Labour says, "in a kindly way", for an explanation that I can give to the people in my riding because, as I see it, the municipality of Chilliwack in which there is a large army camp, and the municipality of Abbotsford, in which there is a great airport, get absolutely nothing. I should like to have an explanation why.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Cases of military establishments will have to be considered on their merits. In respect of a purely self-contained military establishment, where it provides its own municipal services such as roads, fire protection and the like-and there are some of them in Canada-it' is understood that of course they are not being paid the grant in lieu of taxes, because they do not receive municipal services from the particular area in which they are located. There are some of those. Then there are others, such as Esquimalt and, I believe Halifax, where the military property, whether it is navy, army or air force, is within the town limits and is in receipt of general municipal services. Under those circumstances those facts will be taken into account in determining the formula as to whether the grant' would be payable or not.
It is impossible to give a general answer with respect to military and harbour installations without looking at all the circumstances of a particular municipality in which they are located. I am familiar, in a general way, with my hon. friend's constituency, and with at least' one of the large military installations there.

Probably it is because of our climate-and we are noted for our fertility in the Fraser valley-but I would ask the minister, in all seriousness, if there is any hospitalization at Chilliwack for maternity cases. It is all very well for hon. members to scoff at that question, but we have to pay these bills, and we are anxious about it.
I understand that' at the present time the Department of National Health and Welfare are paying for some things in the army camp.
What about hospitalization? I am asking this because I have not the information. I shall be asked about it when I go home, and I think it best to ask the minister at this time. What is the answer, so far as the airport and the army camp in my constituency are concerned? Will consideration be given as circumstances arise?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall have to look into the matter and let my hon. friend know later. Perhaps I can get the information from the Department of National Defence.

I have the honour to represent a Toronto constituency, that of High Park, and I have seen some of the comments that have been made about the minister's statement. I agree thoroughly with the principle enunciated and that we cannot deviate from the principle that has been established from time immemorial that the crown is exempt from taxation. But when we admit that as of grace we are going to make certain payments I am forced with some hesitation to come to the conclusion that I cannot agree with the formula that has been adopted. Once having admitted that principle, I submit that the essential public services that are rendered should be paid for by the federal government.
I notice that water was the only service mentioned, but other services to be considered are police and fire protection, sewage and others. I submit that the proper and businesslike approach would be for the federal government to make these payments on the basis of the services received.
I cannot agree with the inclusion of school taxes because I think that is a provincial responsibility. We have here a resolution which would indicate that we might be asked to do something in that respect in a general way, and I think we should. I associate myself with that principle and I hope that in due course the government will give consideration to it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
This is the statement which deals with the questions and answers thereto:
During the debates on the veterans affairs estimates-Hansard, page 640, column 2 and page 1049, column 1-the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra asked for the number of cases between the period 30th June, 1947, and 30th June, 1949, wherein the commission had refused entitlement on the basis that the condition was pre-enlistment and not aggravated. The total number of such decisions for the two-year period in question is 6,740.
In the course of his remarks the hon. member stated: "and, mind you, they had been discharged as disabled but were ruled out on application for pension on the ground that they had pre-enlistment conditions."
I wish to make it very clear to hon. members that the group in question were not discharged as disabled. The great majority were discharged in the ordinary course of demobilization, and subsequently the Canadian pension commission considered a claim for a condition which may or may not have been recorded on the proceedings of the discharge medical board.
At this stage I find it necessary to say a word regarding the procedure leading up to

Supply-Veterans Affairs these decisions of pre-enlistment origin. On attestation a recruit was medically examined, that examination was a physical one and the examining medical officer asked a number of questions regarding the state of health and as to whether the recruit had ever suffered from certain conditions. This all forms part of the official record on attestation and actually, for example, thousands had defective vision to a greater or lesser degree, but not sufficient to cause rejection. The condition was pre-enlistment and obviously the commission, when considering a claim, would review the discharge board's records and, if there was no worsening during service, would rule "pre-enlistment, not aggravated." In other cases the member of the forces during his service reported sick and gave, on his own volition, a clear-cut statement of the preenlistment existence of the same condition for which he was suffering and being treated. It is the responsibility of the commission to determine whether the condition was, firstly, of pre-enlistment origin and, secondly, if there was any worsening during service; if not, they rule "pre-enlistment, not aggravated." Another group, and quite a considerable one, was found in those cases where, on examination during service, it was found they had constitutional or congenital conditions. These included adolescence and developmental anomalies, all of which were definitely of preenlistment origin, and the commission, on review, had to determined whether service played any part in aggravation.
Again it is only fair I should state that many pre-enlistment conditions were not disclosed as found on enlistment but very soon became apparent and led to discharge. To illustrate, I would repeat the figures on the record of the 1946 committee on veterans affairs: 3,830 served for 30 days or less, 17,388 served from 31 to 90 days, 28,982 served from 91 to 183 days Cwhich is 6 months), 42,516 served from 184 to 364 days. A total of 92,716 men served less than one year because they were found to be unfit and unsuitable for service.
Then again I must point out that the decisions rendered by the commission were initial ones and gave the reasons. The act provides the veteran may renew his claim and may appear before an appeal board of the commission. Not only is this so, but my department has a branch called the veterans' bureau which, free of charge, assists applicants in the preparation and advancement of their claims to pension, and some of the national organizations of ex-servicemen render a similar service.
I make this statement and hope it will make the situation clear regarding this type of claim.

When on the subject, the hon. member for Saskatoon-Hansard, page 641, column 1-[DOT] mentioned the case of a young man who was enlisted for service with the R.C.A.F. and suffers from a severe heart condition which the commission ruled to be of preenlistment origin and they have pensioned on an aggravation basis of two-fifths. On examination I find the facts of this case are:
The applicant had a relatively short period of service in the R.C.A.F., actually less than eight months in Canada. On enlistment he stated he had rheumatic fever in 1934 and later stated he had an earlier one in 1930. No cardiac abnormalities were discovered on enlistment but it was suggested he be watched. He was admitted to hospital less than 6 months after enlistment when the history and diagnosis of heart complications were made and led to his discharge.
It is my understanding that the time at which the heart disease resulting from the rheumatic fever first becomes manifest is a long drawn out process between the stage of original infection and the date of final incapacitation. A most eminent specialist says: "It is to the growing child we must go as rheumatic heart disease begins always in childhood." It certainly did in this case at the ages of eleven and fifteen.
We therefore have an airman who, very soon after enlistment, gave evidence of the serious effects of two childhood attacks of rheumatic fever. He had no complaints at the time of his discharge from service, no murmurs were detected and he worked as a C.P.R. brakeman until December, 1944, when he had a further recurrence of joint pains and definite murmurs were described. The commission has ruled pre-enlistment, aggravated to the extent of two-fifths of his entire disability. The latter is assessed at 100 per cent, and two-fifths of that is 40 per cent, being the award in payment. He also has the right to treatment with hospital allowances from my department at any time such is required.

Question by hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough-(Hansard, page 2617):
Will the minister tell us how many departments there are in Ontario and just how an application goes through? Will he explain what causes the long delay?
Answer:	The province of Ontario, for
administrative purposes, is divided into two districts, eastern Ontario and western Ontario, with the district offices for each being in Toronto and London respectively. Under the Toronto district office, there are five regional offices and two subregional offices. In eastern Ontario, there are four regional offices. This does not cover the Port Arthur -Fort William area which is under the jurisdiction of Winnipeg district office and which area is administered by one regional office.
An application goes through in the following manner: the veteran makes application to a regional office for certification that he is qualified to receive the benefits of the Veterans Land Act. After checking on the vete^pn's eligibility as to sufficient war service and receiving replies from the references given by the veteran at the time of his application, the veteran appears before a regional advisory committee for qualification. Subsequent to being qualified for assistance under the Veterans Land Act, the veteran submits an application for assistance with respect to the particular property on which he desires establishment. Upon receipt of this application, an appraisal is made of the property by the department. If the appraisal indicates the property is suitable, action is taken towards its purchase. As soon as the director has obtained title to the property, it is then resold to the veteran by agreement for sale.
During consideration in committee, I undertook to indicate the average time taken for an application to go through after acceptance. Accurate statistics on this point are not maintained by the department but a check made during the month of September last of a mill run of 100 cases showed the following to be the situation:-from the date an application was approved until title was registered in the director, the average number of days which elapsed in western Ontario was 65, in eastern Ontario 100, in Quebec 99, and in the maritime provinces 37. In the prairie provinces and B.C., the average number of days was only 27 [DOT] 6. Members of the legal profession in the house will appreciate that this wide spread probably may be largely attributed to the different land registration systems which obtain in the provinces. There are, of course, other factors involved. Often there are defects in the vendor's title which cannot be remedied without some formal

application to a registrar of titles or to a probate court or the employment of a surveyor to determine the boundaries of the land to be conveyed. There is sometimes loss of time in searching for heirs or others who may have some interest in the land and who must sign the documents of release.

This is the hospitalization item. Earlier in the session the suggestion was made that hospitalization might be provided for the men of the merchant navy without the amendment of any statute because of the wide terms of the act which set up the Department of Veterans Affairs. That act gives the department power to help those who were associated in the war. It is not restricted in the same way as the Pension Act. Can the parliamentary assistant tell us whether consideration has been given to providing hospitalization for these unfortunate men? I would point out to him that, to all intents and purposes, it was practically impossible for a man in the merchant navy to qualify for a pension on the ground of disease. Even to qualify on the ground of injury he had to trace the injury to enemy action.
It is practically impossible for a man to qualify because of diseases such as malaria, tuberculosis, and so on. I know personally of quite a few sad cases where young lads have developed tuberculosis, obviously because of their service at sea with the

929. War veterans allowance board-administration-further amount required, $11,000.

This item has to do with war veterans allowance. As the committee knows, the present position is that the maximum war veterans allowance which can be paid to a single man is $40.41 a month, and the maximum for a married man is $70.83 a month. In addition to that there was a vote in the sum of $500,000 which provided for further assistance. It was called a special assistance fund. On November 8 I had the answers to some questions concerning this fund, as follows:
1.	How many veterans were in receipt of war veterans allowance as of October 31, 1949?
Answer: 25,918.
2.	How many of such recipients have made application for assistance from the special assistance fund?
Answer: 3,174.
[Mr. Gillis.J

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Nothing like one in ten have asked for it.

The reason more have not asked for it is the restrictions. That fund can be used only in the case of a recipient of war veterans allowance who is drawing the full amount. If he is getting a partial allowance then under the regulations he has no right to ask for help from this special fund. Another reason that more veterans have not asked for it is that to get any help they have to go through a second means test, which they bitterly resent. As the committee knows, they have to pass a means test to qualify in the first place; then before they can qualify for further assistance they have to pass another means test. I have here the instructions sent out by the department to their officers for completing applications for this special assistance, and I am going to read paragraph 13:
Consultation with social service division may be indicated in completing this paragraph. Entitlement of all members of the family group should be explored, particularly those of dependents. For example, the wife may be seventy years or over and thus entitled to old age pension, which generally carries with it the right to medical and hospital care, and it might be in the veteran's interest to go on single rate and his wife on old age pension. Again, there may be an unmet health need for which a resource is available in the community.
That paragraph illustrates the tragedy about this whole special assistance fund; namely, that the veteran probably will be better off if he can get on the old age pension, or if he can get his wife on it. Surely that is not the way Canada wants to treat her veterans. I am sure the Canadian people would disagree violently with a policy of that kind. These recipients of the war veterans allowance were front line men. If they had not seen action they could not qualify, except for a small percentage with disability pensions who did not get to the front line areas. Practically all these veterans were Canada's fighting men of the first great war; and eventually, mind you, the men of the second world war will qualify in the same way. That is the actual position. In some cases today these men are better off not to take the war veterans allowance and they go on the old age pension. I have here an editorial from the Vancouver Sun of November 12 of this year entitled "Burnt out and burnt up." This was written the day after Armistice day. The newspaper office is

within a short distance of the Vancouver war memorial, and these older veterans had been attending the parade, as they usually do. The editorial points out:
They are today In a worse position than old age pensioners. Both are supported from public funds. Why in the name of all that is reasonable should those who made special sacrifices for their country be subsequently penalized? Surely the least that could be done is set the WVA rate at a figure equal to the OAP, even if the former may qualify before age seventy.
It goes on to point out:
Needy veterans now get $40 a month war veterans allowance; their wives $30-a total of $70.
Actually the total for man and wife is $70.83.
The veteran, if sick, can get treatment in a DVA hospital with $15 deducted from the pension for each month, but wives and dependents are compelled, from their meagre income, to pay into B.C.'s provincial hospital insurance fund.
A man and wife together on OAP get $100 monthly in British Columbia and are entitled to provincial hospitalization while exempt from premiums. But a veteran's wife and children, under this ridiculous system, are penalized and can be haled into court and fined for non-payment of hospital premiums out of their pittance.
Then it further says:
Some wives of older veterans are voluntarily abandoning their $30 WVA allowance to claim an old age pension. Obviously, however, only a few of them are old enough to do so.
I realize that this special assistance fund was brought in as a temporary measure, but I suggest to the government that the time has now come when the situation can only be met by increasing the war veterans allowance by statute. Just a few weeks ago the Canadian Legion made representations to the government. They also made representations to members of the house on December 5, in which they asked that the war veterans allowance be increased from $40 to $50 monthly for a single veteran and from $70 to $85 monthly for a married veteran. I do hope action of that kind will be taken at the next session. I am sure every veteran member of the House of Commons, regardless of party, would support that suggestion.
Then I should like to say a word about the group of men called the imperial veterans. Year in and year out we have been urging that they be made eligible for the war veterans allowance, but as yet they have not been granted that entitlement. The Legion deals with their position also and points out that since Newfoundland has come into confederation the imperials in that province have been made eligible for Canadian war veterans allowance, and quite properly so. We ask that this right be extended at the next session to the imperials living in the other provinces of Canada. Personally I would hope that all the men who served in 45781-199
Supply-Veterans Affairs the forces of the King and who have been here for a period of years would be made eligible. I believe we should also include those who served in the forces of France and Belgium, who were our allies in the first war. The Legion points out that a survey was made this year by the Department of Veterans Affairs to ascertain the number of imperials who would benefit and that there are only 2,311 known cases who would become eligible. In their brief they suggest that it could very well be assumed that the total would not be in excess of 3,000. So I hope that at the next session these men will be made eligible.
There is also the question of the treatment of the merchant navy veterans. I need not repeat tonight what I have said about them before, but their situation is very unfair.
It all adds up to this. We do not believe we will get any of these improvements unless a special committee is set up next session. Even then we may not get all the improvements, but certainly past experience has shown that there is unlikely to be any veterans legislation amounting to much unless there is a special committee of the house on veterans affairs. We have not had one this session. We have in the house a very large number of returned men of both the recent war and the first war. I would ask the parliamentary assistant if he can give us an assurance tonight that next session a special committee on veterans affairs will be set up.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre inquired on Friday evening, the 9th of December, 1949, about the financial arrangements for the payment of old age pensions in the Yukon territory. No discretion of th minister was involved. It was the duty o the minister not only to see that the report wa made public, but certainly to do nothing tha would prevent its being made public.
It is certain, of course, that what has bee: done cannot be undone and cannot be changec It never can. Our task as members of thi house is to consider what should be done as result of what has happened and what can not be changed. It was not inadvertence. Th question of publication was not one fc discretion. The minister was informed, an this was not made public until more tha ten months after it had been completed. 1 was not made public because the ministe had decided it was not going to be mad public, for reasons that had nothing to d with pressure of time or inadvertence.
The suggestion of the Prime Minister is the once a law has been broken it cannot b broken any more; and if by inadvertence th time has passed within which somethin should be done, then that is all that ca happen. If this principle were applied to th income tax requirements, then if for an reason someone failed to file an income ta return he might just as well go ahead an not only continue to fail to file it but n< make the payments required under the ac
What is involved here is not just tl question of failure to make public. A numbi of other results would have flowed fro: making the report public as soon as th; could be done, whether or not it was withi the fifteen days. If the report had been mac public at any time within three months of tl date required by statute, the previous parlii ment still would have been sitting and tl house could have dealt appropriately with tl information that was made available. >f knowing the facts in this particular case >efore passing judgment at the polls. Third, f the report had been made public within en months, then others might have launched xrosecutions if they thought that was the proper course, based upon the evidence :ontained in the report.
This is no mere case of a technical breach >f the statutory requirements, as was :uggested by the Minister of Justice in his extraordinary statement yesterday. There was a breach of the statutory require-nent in that case; but, important though it vas that the members of this house should lave known what the maritime commission ;aid, within fifteen days of the opening of ;he session, which was required by statute, there can be no suggestion that in that nstance the circumstances were similar. The action of the government in this case lid these things: First, it denied to the public nformation the public was entitled to have ast January. Those were the consequences which flowed from this act. It was not just a case of some delay in the information being made available. These were the direct results not of inadvertence but of the deliberate act of the government itself. It is important to go back to the time when the act in its present form was introduced. Because he was the man responsible for bringing in the act at that time, I should like to quote briefly from the words of the prime minister of Canada of that day, Mr. Mackenzie King, as they appear at page 2605 of Hansard for May 8, 1923:
What is the power of the Criminal Code to prosecute some particular person or group of persons in comparison with the power of spreading broadcast throughout the land accurate and true information with regard to a situation which is inimical to the public interest, and which the people themselves are certain to be concerned in remedying? relation to the subject matter of this report. By the deliberate and calculated act of the government, the time lapsed within which any prosecution could be launched by anyone.
At a later date, dealing with the question of publication of reports, Mr. Ilsley has this to say, as reported at page 3473 of Hansard of 1935.
An intolerable condition exists when we permit the making of expensive and important inquiries into alleged combines and have the reports kept secret.
I think that sums up the situation. An intolerable situation exists when any report of an inquiry of this kind is held back and not made available to the members of parliament, who have a duty and a right to act with knowledge of what that report contains. I do not think a more flagrant violation of this or any other act passed by parliament could possibly be conceived. It still seems that the Minister of Justice, the members of the government, and many of the members of this house fail to recognize that this is no technicality. This is no mere procedural problem, nor is it just a case of inadvertence. They fail to recognize that a fundamental issue is involved here; that what has happened cannot be changed.
If that fundamental principle is to be respected, then something must be done. If we were asked what is the real guarantee of our liberty, I think that the most of us who have studied our constitutional history would answer: the equality of every Canadian under the law. If we were asked how that equality under the law can be assured, we would surely answer that the rule of law must be respected by every Canadian, from the Prime Minister down to the humblest citizen; that is the simple but unescapable issue before us. A law of this parliament has been broken, and deliberately broken, by the Minister of Justice. While it is true that the government has concurred in and must share the responsibility, as Minister of Justice he is charged with the enforcement of law. He stands in a special position in relation to the enforcement of this or any other law.
The Minister of Justice has broken this law, and that fact cannot be changed. For that reason, respect for the laws of this parliament and the enforcement of those laws can be restored only when the present Minister of Justice ceases to occupy that position.

I wish to agree in principle with all that has been said by the leader of the official opposition. I have been interested in this subject, because for a great many years it was my duty and my privilege

Supply-Justice
to hold up before young Canadians in this country the high standard of the British parliamentary system, British law and justice. It is because this incident which we are discussing now seems to me to undermine the whole structure of the British parliamentary system that I feel concerned about it.
I regret very much that the Minister of Justice has, by a series of circumstances over which he may or may not have had any control, become involved in this situation. It is not my wish that any hon. member of the Liberal party, or any other party, should find himself in such a position.
The leader of the official opposition has just pointed out that it is not simply a failure to comply with the regulations. What I cannot forgive the Minister of Justice for- or for that matter the Minister of Trade and Commerce, or the Prime Minister, because both have accepted responsibility for the course of action followed-is not their failure, because of the pressure of time, to make this report public, but the fact that those gentlemen sat through a whole session of parliament, which lasted for three months, knowing that they were withholding information. They failed to take parliament into their confidence. Following that, they went before the country in a general election, and withheld from the public, until they were safely back in office, the information which the public should have had. A series of byelections were held, also, before the information was revealed. That is not fair, either to parliament or to the people of Canada.
In my humble opinion there is only one course that the Minister of Justice can take if he has any regard for the maintenance of our laws, if he has any respect for the responsibility of a cabinet or cabinet ministers to parliament, and that is for him to tender his resignation to the governor general. So far as that goes, I can see very little difference between the conduct of the Minister of Justice and that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Prime Minister. Both have openly-

I may say to the Liberal backbenchers that this is no laughing matter. Even the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice laugh, as though this were an everyday occurrence. I am giving my opinion as one who has some regard for the rights of parliament and respect for the laws of our country. I say this, Mr. Chairman, that if any other member of this House of Commons had followed the same course and deliberately flouted legislation passed by this parliament, the Minister of Justice could follow no other *ourse. if he were to fulfil his duties, than

to have that member unseated. I submit that is the only course that the Minister of Justice can follow.

The reduction in those items accounts for the net reduction in the amount of the estimate. There is no actual reduction in the amount of money currently expended on the prisoners' welfare.

Under the present penitentiary regulations, prisoners suffering from a communicable disease or one that requires active treatment are paroled out to an institution. On the other hand, there have come to my attention recently cases in which prisoners who were sentenced were suffering from a communicable disease, and in which the penitentiary authorities refused to admit them. Recently there were brought to my attention two cases, from Halifax, of veterans who got into difficulties, who were sentenced to two years' imprisonment and who required active treatment for t.b., but the penitentiary would not take them in. There was quite a bit of difficulty in having the matter resolved. I think the minister's department should consider amendment of the regulations to provide for the establishment of some central institution in Canada to which prisoners of that type may be sent. While this crime may not have been very serious, it was bad enough. What happens when a man is sentenced for murder, manslaughter or some other serious crime of that nature? In Canada if he is sentenced to a penitentiary, there is no place which will accept him. I know there must be a lot of cases across the country because in the last eight months I have run across three of them. Has this been brought to the minister's attention, and is the department considering any remedial action?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

This matter has arisen in a minor way from time to time, but there has been no concerted effort upon the part of

Ways and Means
the provinces, who are the interested parties -because the expense of this treatment falls upon, them-to request that we should do this. In point of fact, in view of the total convict population of our penitentiaries, the treatment of tuberculosis by us would be a much more expensive way of providing such treatment for those who are suffering from it than to let them take their treatment in provincial institutions.

speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether it is intended to do anything about the Senate amendments to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Macnaughton) to amend the Canadian Red Cross Society Act? speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am told that the Senate amendments have not been printed, and hon. members have not had an opportunity of seeing them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Hon. members could find out quite easily what the amendments are, because all the Senate did was to strike out the first two sections. There is nothing left
Mr. Garson.]

but the third section. I must be careful in what I say, but I want to protest against what was done over there.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am informed that the reason for the amendments made by the Senate was that there was no one available to answer questions they put with respect to the extent of the immovable property now producing revenue for the society. I am told that the intention was to delete that clause, because they could not get the information required and there was no. urgency about the other provisions of the bill.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The other action taken by the Senate was to cut out the section that provided for such changes as were necessary to bring Newfoundland into the Canadian Red Cross. It seems to me that the action taken over there was rather high-handed.
I think it is obvious that the desires of the Red Cross would not be satisfied if we adopted the bill in its amended form.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is my understanding. It would probably better suit their convenience to have whatever amendments they wish made to their act included in the one bill, and not have the bill introduced by the member for Mount Royal, in its emasculated form, adopted at this time.

Prorogation of Parliament twenty-first parliament of the Dominion of Canada with the following speech:
Honourable Members of the Senate:
Members of the House of Commons:
Since the opening the present session of parliament you have approved measures required for the discharge of the constitutional responsibilities of our nationhood. As a result the Supreme Court of Canada will shortly become the final court of appeal for Canada.
In response to your address the parliament of the United Kingdom has amended the British North America Act to vest in the parliament of Canada the power to make amendments to the constitution of Canada in matters which are exclusively of federal concern.
Early in the new year a conference with representatives of the provincial governments will be held for the purpose of working out a satisfactory procedure for making within Canada such other amendments to the constitution as may from time to time be required.
Our country continues to take an active part in the proceedings of the United Nations. Despite that organization's present inability to solve the major political problem confronting mankind, the United Nations has succeeded in coping with menacing situations in many parts of the world. At the current session of the general assembly, Canada was elected to the economic and social council.
It is gratifying that the agencies under the North Atlantic treaty have been established and are undertaking the tasks which have been assigned to them.
My ministers are giving constant attention to the defence needs of Canada. The consideration of the measure to consolidate existing legislation respecting our defence forces has not been completed. This measure will be re-introduced at your next session.
The real foundation of the ability of the nations of the north Atlantic community to defend themselves lies in their continued economic strength and stability. Canada is co-operating with other nations, particularly the United Kingdom and the United States, in seeking solutions to the difficult economic problems which still confront the democratic world.
The revaluation of currencies in western Europe and the sterling area made it necessary to alter the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar.
You have approved important amendments to the National Housing Act designed to maintain the present high volume of housing construction.
Legislation has also been enacted to enable the federal government to enter into agreements with the provinces for sharing the cost of construction of a trans-Canada highway.
Provision has been made for three new departments to replace the Department of Reconstruction and Supply and the Department of Mines and Resources. These will be the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Department of Resources and Development, and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration which will also be responsible for the administration of Indian affairs.
A special parliamentary committee examined into the operations of the atomic energy control board.
During the session measures have been enacted respecting forest conservation; the application of a national trade mark and the true description of commodities; the establishment of the Canadian Overseas Telecommunication Corporation; assistance
in the production of coal in the Atlantic maritime region; encouragement of the construction of ships in Canada; the disposal of surplus crown assets. Amendments have been made to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act of 1939; the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; the Industrial Development Bank Act; the Criminal Code; the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act; the Judges Act of 1946; the Animal Contagious Diseases Act; the Export and Import Permits Act; and the Veterans Land Act of 1942. The fish inspection legislation has been revised. The Combines Investigation Act has been strengthened and a complete revision has been made of the Bankruptcy Act.
The government has announced a new policy respecting grants to municipalities in which there is an exceptional concentration of federal property.
Members of the House of Commons:
I thank you for the provision you have made for all essential services for the current fiscal year. The budget resolutions, providing for substantial reductions in taxation, have been approved and the necessary legislation has been enacted.
Honourable Members of the Senate:
Members of the House of Commons:
As you return to your homes, I should like to extend to you and through you to those you represent my best wishes for the Christmas season and to express the hope that Divine Providence will continue to bless our people with prosperity and happiness in the New Year.

Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent,

subsubtopic: FURTHER CORRESPONDENCE WITH PREMIERS OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
The members of the executive council of the province have learned from your letter of November 7, which was delivered to my office yesterday afternoon, that the opening session of the dominion-provincial conference which "will consider means to amend the constitution of Canada" will be held in Ottawa on the 10th of January, 1950, at 10.30 a.m.
I presume that the precise place where the sessions of the conference will take place will be determined in the near future.
Yours sincerely,
M. L. Duplessis
OFFICE OF THE PRIME MINISTER Canada
Ottawa, November 15, 1949
Hon. Maurice Duplessis, M.L.A.,	.
Premier of Quebec,
Quebec, Que.
My dear Premier:
I duly received your letter of the 9th instant inquiring as to the exact place where the sittings of the proposed constitutional conference would be held. The government will arrange to hold the opening meeting in the centre block of the parliament buildings, and all the premiers will be advised in advance of the precise room and other arrangements.
Yours sincerely,
Louis S. St. Laurent
PREMIER'S OFFICE Saskatchewan
Regina, November 29, 1949
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ont.
My dear Prime Minister:
Thank you for your recent letter confirming the January 10 date for the dominion-provincial conference to consider a method of amending
the constitution of Canada. It is felt here that different techniques may be required for different matters. If this be so, it would be difficult to consider the question of amendment in a general way. I would therefore be very much obliged if you could send me the proposed agenda. I am certain you will understand the difficulty with which we are faced in trying to do preparatory work before knowing what items are coming up for discussion and what the method of procedure will be. I note, too, that a preliminary meeting of constitutional experts, in advance of the main conference, is not to be held. This fact necessitates our having a proposed agenda as soon as possible.
Trusting you will be able to assist us by forwarding an agenda to us at your earliest convenience, I remain,
Yours sincerely,
T. C. Douglas
OFFICE OF THE PRIME MINISTER AND PRESIDENT OF THE COUNCIL Ontario
Toronto, December 8, 1949
Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, K.C.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Canada.
My dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I have your letter of the 7th instant.
My feeling is that the reduction of the subject matter of the conference opening January 10 to an agenda of procedure is not necessary. I think better progress will be made if the question of procedure in the conference is left until the conference itself convenes. These matters can then be considered and settled. If in the meantime any of the other provinces have suggestions to make in this regard, I should be glad indeed if you would advise me. My feeling at the moment is that a formal agenda is not necessary.
Concerning your proposal that a general provincial conference should be held early in the autumn of 1950, possibly in September or October, I am in agreement. In this case the situation is quite different and there are many matters which the various provinces will probably be anxious to have discussed. In this case an agenda of subject matters should be prepared in advance, although I believe as much of the procedure as possible should be left to the conference itself. I shall be glad to discuss this matter with you at any time.
Yours very truly,
Leslie M. Frost
